is several actions and the unique case is one that `source.fixAll.nvs` may apply on save. Three names get
no fix at all: a qualified one, because it is absolute and no import changes what it means
([`statements/a-qualified-name-is-absolute`](statements.md#statements-a-qualified-name-is-absolute)); a short name an existing `use` already resolves to
something undeclared, because that import is the mistake and a second `use` of the same short name would
not compile; and one written in a file with no place to put the line — a bracketed namespace with no
`use` in it, a script with no open tag — because the checker names a place or none, and never invents
one.

What it spends is a walk over the symbol table and the registry on the checker's error path, and
nothing on a program that compiles.

**Declined:**
- **A fix the server computes from the diagnostic's span.** It is a fix no diagnostic carries
  ([`ide/a-code-action-ships-only-a-fix-a-diagnostic-already-knows`](ide.md#ide-a-code-action-ships-only-a-fix-a-diagnostic-already-knows)), and it would be a second
  implementation of the name resolution `definition` already applies.
- **Replacing the written name with its qualified spelling.** It is determined and cheap, but a developer
  who wrote a short name wanted a `use` line, not a file full of qualified names.

<sub>See also [`ide/a-code-action-ships-only-a-fix-a-diagnostic-already-knows`](ide.md#ide-a-code-action-ships-only-a-fix-a-diagnostic-already-knows), [`ide/a-code-action-writes-only-what-is-already-determined`](ide.md#ide-a-code-action-writes-only-what-is-already-determined), [`ide/a-bare-name-reaches-every-type-and-imports-the-one-accepted`](ide.md#ide-a-bare-name-reaches-every-type-and-imports-the-one-accepted), [`ide/a-pasted-type-carries-its-use-line`](ide.md#ide-a-pasted-type-carries-its-use-line), [`statements/a-qualified-name-is-absolute`](statements.md#statements-a-qualified-name-is-absolute).</sub>

<a id="ide-a-pasted-type-carries-its-use-line"></a>

## A type name pasted from one file into another brings the `use` line that resolves it, read at copy time from the file it came from

`rule:ide/a-pasted-type-carries-its-use-line`

A type name pasted from one `.nvs` file into another brings the `use` line that makes it resolve there,
read at copy time from the file it came from. Two requests of Novis's own carry it: `nvs/imports`, asked
in the source document when text is copied, answers every type name the copied range wrote — the receiver
of a `::` access, the class after `new`, every name in an annotation — paired with what it resolved to
through that file's imports and namespace, and the editor keeps the answer on the clipboard beside the
text under a MIME type of the extension's own. `nvs/importEdits`, asked in the destination when that
clipboard is pasted, takes those pairs and the paste position and answers the `use` lines the destination
lacks, as one edit at the place every `use` line this server writes goes
([`ide/a-bare-name-reaches-every-type-and-imports-the-one-accepted`](ide.md#ide-a-bare-name-reaches-every-type-and-imports-the-one-accepted)'s place, `nvs_hir::imports`).

**What is carried is what the source resolved, never what the text looks like.** A name is put through
the same lookup a click follows, with the namespace and the imports in force at the position it was
written; one that resolves to nothing declared is not carried, because importing it fixes nothing, and a
qualified name is carried as written and imported nowhere, because it is absolute
([`statements/a-qualified-name-is-absolute`](statements.md#statements-a-qualified-name-is-absolute)). At the destination a name is imported only where it
would not resolve as it was written — a namespace that already reaches it, or a `use` already in force,
means no line — and only under a short name nothing there already answers to; a name that cannot be
imported is left as the paste wrote it, and the checker's own diagnostic on it offers the fix
([`ide/an-undeclared-name-offers-its-import`](ide.md#ide-an-undeclared-name-offers-its-import)).

**The paste is the editor's, not a command.** The edit is offered under the `text.updateImports` kind,
and because the editor applies a provider's edit on its own only for a kind its
`editor.pasteAs.preferences` names — a list that is empty by default — the extension contributes
`["text.updateImports"]` as that setting's default for Novis documents. So the import arrives with the
paste and nothing is added to a menu, a keymap or the extension's own settings
([`ide/the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has`](ide.md#ide-the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has)); a user who wants plain text back
overrides that preference, and the edit is then offered in the editor's paste widget instead. A paste that needs no import, a clipboard that carries no answer of the
extension's, and a server that is not running are all the editor's ordinary paste. The copy-time ask is
what makes a paste into another window, or after the source was closed or edited, still correct: what
the text meant is a fact about the file as it was at the copy. Each client owns its own copy of the two
asks ([`ide/one-server-two-thin-clients`](ide.md#ide-one-server-two-thin-clients)).

What it spends is one analysis of the source at copy time and one of the destination at paste time, both
of documents the server already holds, and nothing between the two. The two answers have no `.lspt`
spelling — a list of name pairs and a text edit — and are held by a Rust test on the wire shapes instead
([`ide/an-lsp-answer-is-frozen-as-an-lspt-case`](ide.md#ide-an-lsp-answer-is-frozen-as-an-lspt-case)).

**Declined:**
- **One request at paste time that re-reads the source.** By then the source may be closed, edited or
  in another window. The clipboard is the only place the copy-time fact survives.

<sub>See also [`ide/the-request-set-is-closed`](ide.md#ide-the-request-set-is-closed), [`ide/a-bare-name-reaches-every-type-and-imports-the-one-accepted`](ide.md#ide-a-bare-name-reaches-every-type-and-imports-the-one-accepted), [`ide/an-undeclared-name-offers-its-import`](ide.md#ide-an-undeclared-name-offers-its-import), [`ide/the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has`](ide.md#ide-the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has), [`ide/one-server-two-thin-clients`](ide.md#ide-one-server-two-thin-clients).</sub>

<a id="ide-a-code-action-writes-only-what-is-already-determined"></a>

## A code action that writes may write only text the type system has already fully determined, and never makes a choice

`rule:ide/a-code-action-writes-only-what-is-already-determined`

Four code actions **write** rather than fix, and one bound governs all of them: an action may write only
text the type system has already fully determined. It never invents a body, never names a parameter from a
heuristic, and never picks between two possible signatures. Anything needing a choice is a refactoring
the user drives, not an action a light bulb offers.

The four: **implement missing members** — on a class that does not satisfy an interface or abstract
base, insert every missing method with the signature copied from the declaration,
[`statements/inout-is-the-by-reference-spelling`](statements.md#statements-inout-is-the-by-reference-spelling) markers and qualifiers intact, and a body that
throws; **override a method** — one action per overridable member of the hierarchy, inserting that
signature with a call to the base; **declare the method you just called** — on the
unresolved-call diagnostic, insert a method on the receiver's class, since Novis has no free function
(`E0215`, `E0320`), whose parameter types are the argument types at the call and whose return type is the
one the context requires, both already computed to produce the diagnostic;
and **narrow an `array<mixed>` to its literal's type**
([`ide/narrow-an-annotation-to-its-literal`](ide.md#ide-narrow-an-annotation-to-its-literal)), which writes an annotation rather than a declaration
under the same bound.

Applying a generator produces text that compiles, and applying it twice is a no-op. Implementing
missing members is the most-used action of its kind in PHP editors, and Novis's explicit types make
it mechanical where PHP's make it a guess. A class with it applied passes `nvs check` with only the
inserted `throw`s reachable.

**Getter/setter generation is refused** under this bound and under [`classes/property-observer`](classes.md#classes-property-observer):
property hooks mean the pair of methods that action exists to save typing has no reason to be written.
Code snippets are refused for a neighbouring reason — a snippet body is a second copy of a syntactic shape
the grammar already owns, silently stale after a grammar change.

**Built:** implement missing members and override a method (`crates/nvs-lsp/src/generate.rs`).
Implement missing members is a `quickfix` on `E0449`, the one diagnostic for a method an interface or
an `abstract` parent leaves without a body; the checker owes no property, so it writes methods. Each
signature is the declaration's own text with each type written the way the class's file names it,
and the body throws a `LogicError`. Override a method is a `refactor.rewrite` action at a cursor
between a class's members, one per method with a body that a class above it declares and that is not
`private`, `final`, `static`, the constructor, or one with an `inout` parameter. Its body calls
`parent::` and returns what that returns, unless the return type is `void` or `never`. Both actions
analyse the text they write and are offered only when it reports no error, which is what makes the
text compile and makes a second application offer nothing: the class then reports no `E0449`, and
declares every method an override would write.

Declare the method you just called is a `quickfix` on the `E0405` of `$obj->name(...)`, offered when the
entry document declares the receiver's class. The checker records the argument types and the type the
context expects beside that diagnostic (`nvs_types::expr_table::UnresolvedCall`), and records nothing for
a program that compiles. A literal argument gives its plain type. The method is `private` when the call
is inside the class and `public` otherwise. A parameter is named after a named argument or a variable
argument, and `$argN` otherwise. With no expectation, the return type is `void` where the call starts a
statement and `mixed` elsewhere. The body throws a `LogicError`, and the text is analysed before it is
offered. A static call and a `...` spread get nothing. Applied once, the call resolves, so a second
application finds no diagnostic.

Narrow an `array<mixed>` is a `refactor.rewrite` at the annotation (`crates/nvs-lsp/src/narrow.rs`). The
type it writes is the one the checker recorded for the literal, and the document with the edit applied
must report the diagnostics it reported before. Applied once, the annotation is no longer
`array<mixed>`, so a second application finds nothing to offer.

<sub>See also [`ide/narrowing-is-a-diff-never-a-save-time-fix`](ide.md#ide-narrowing-is-a-diff-never-a-save-time-fix), [`classes/property-observer`](classes.md#classes-property-observer), [`statements/inout-is-the-by-reference-spelling`](statements.md#statements-inout-is-the-by-reference-spelling), [`routing/a-quick-fix-writes-a-derived-path`](routing.md#routing-a-quick-fix-writes-a-derived-path), [`ide/every-feature-is-staged-behind-its-dependency`](ide.md#ide-every-feature-is-staged-behind-its-dependency).</sub>

<a id="ide-no-refactoring-introduces-an-alias"></a>

## Rename, organize-imports and auto-import never write a `use` alias: an import inserts the fully-qualified name, and organize-imports only reorders and removes

`rule:ide/no-refactoring-introduces-an-alias`

The refactorings are LSP requests — workspace-wide rename, extract to method or variable, and
organize-imports — and the deeper completion is signature help, cross-file symbol search, auto-import,
and inlay hints for `var`-inferred types ([`types/var-inference`](types.md#types-var-inference)) and call-site parameter names.

None of them writes an alias. Organize-imports is restricted to reordering and removing unused `use`
statements; auto-import inserts the correct fully-qualified name and nothing else. An editor that
resolved a clash with `use Foo as Bar` would be inventing a spelling the language does not have
([`statements/nothing-gets-a-second-name`](statements.md#statements-nothing-gets-a-second-name)), and a second name introduced by tooling is exactly as
much a second name as one typed by hand.

**Built:** signature help, inlay hints, and the three places the server writes a `use` line: an
accepted completion, a pasted type ([`ide/a-pasted-type-carries-its-use-line`](ide.md#ide-a-pasted-type-carries-its-use-line)) and an undeclared
name's fix. Each writes the fully-qualified name at `nvs_hir::import_site` and never an alias
(`crates/nvs-lsp/src/imports.rs`). Rename of a member or a local, and the `require` paths a moved file
changes (`crates/nvs-lsp/src/rename.rs`): a method is renamed with every method that overrides it or
that it overrides, and a new name that some class of that family, above it or below it, already
declares is refused with a message. A local's new name may not be bound already in its body. Neither
is ever resolved with an alias. Rename of a class, an interface, an enum or a type alias declared
outside a class: the index records each type annotation and each class written in front of `::`, and
the rename changes the last segment at every site and in every `use` line. A new name that another
type in the workspace has, or that a file with a site already writes, is refused. A type declared
alone in a file named after it renames that file with it, so an `autoload` still finds it.
Organize imports, a `source.organizeImports` code action (`crates/nvs-lsp/src/organize.rs`): it deletes
each `use` line the `W1026` warning reports, with that warning's own edit, and sorts the rest with
`nvs fmt`'s sort, so a format after it moves nothing. Cross-file symbol search: `workspace/symbol`
reads the reference index's declarations.
Extract to variable and extract to method, two `refactor.extract` code actions over a selection
(`crates/nvs-lsp/src/extract.rs`). Extract to variable writes a typed local declaration on its own
line above the statement, and replaces the selected expression with the variable. Extract to method
writes a `private` method after the one the selection is in, and replaces the selection with a call to
it. Its parameters are the locals the selection reads, with the types they were declared with. Its
return type is the selected expression's, and `void` for a run of whole statements. An expression's
type is the one the checker gives `var $name = <selection>;` written above its statement, and each
action is offered only once the text it writes analyses with no error, so a document that already
reports one is offered neither.

The boundary of extract to method is one exit and no write that escapes. A selection holding a
`return`, `yield` or `goto`, or a `break` or `continue` with no loop around it inside the selection, is
offered nothing, and so is one that assigns or increments a local declared before it, or passes one as
`inout` or `&`. Writing such a method would mean choosing an `inout` parameter or a result to unpack,
which is a choice and not a fact. A selection inside an anonymous function, or holding one, is refused
too. Extract to variable keeps its own boundary: it is refused where moving the expression above its
statement changes when it runs — a loop condition, an `elseif`, the right side of `&&`, `||` or `??`, a
branch of `?:` or `match`, and after `?->`. Both refuse an assignment's target, an increment's operand,
the operand of `isset`, `empty` and `unset`, and a bare variable. Each analysis is of the editor's own
graph and runs only while a selection covers exactly one expression or run of statements.

<sub>See also [`statements/nothing-gets-a-second-name`](statements.md#statements-nothing-gets-a-second-name), [`types/var-inference`](types.md#types-var-inference), [`ide/every-feature-is-staged-behind-its-dependency`](ide.md#ide-every-feature-is-staged-behind-its-dependency), [`ide/five-features-are-one-reference-index`](ide.md#ide-five-features-are-one-reference-index).</sub>

<a id="ide-narrow-an-annotation-to-its-literal"></a>

## One editor action rewrites an `array<mixed>` annotation to the type of the array literal that initializes it, and rewrites nothing else

`rule:ide/narrow-an-annotation-to-its-literal`

A deep nested literal gets annotated `array<mixed>` because writing `array<array<array<float>>>` by hand
is tedious, and the annotation then costs the program the typed path for the rest of its life: every
operation on a `mixed` resolves through the generic helper path, every element write becomes a runtime
check, and every read out of the structure needs an `as` at the far end. The type is derivable — the
checker already walks every element — so one editor action derives it.

The action is offered on the **type annotation** of a declaration whose initializer is an **array literal
in the same file**. It rewrites that annotation and nothing else — not the literal, not a use site, not
another line. It is invoked by the developer from the annotation; there is no diagnostic and no hint
behind it, because nothing is wrong, and discoverability rides on the annotation's own light bulb. It
never changes a value's kind: a union in the offer such as `array<string|int|array<string>>` is a signal
that the value is a record and wants an object shape, but converting the literal is not this action's
business, because it would turn copy-on-write value semantics into shared-reference ones.

What it writes is decided by [`ide/narrowest-means-narrowest-base-type`](ide.md#ide-narrowest-means-narrowest-base-type); when it declines, by
[`ide/the-action-answers-from-the-literal-or-not-at-all`](ide.md#ide-the-action-answers-from-the-literal-or-not-at-all); and why it never runs on save, by
[`ide/narrowing-is-a-diff-never-a-save-time-fix`](ide.md#ide-narrowing-is-a-diff-never-a-save-time-fix). It is a code action whose fix the checker has to
compute, which places it under [`ide/a-code-action-writes-only-what-is-already-determined`](ide.md#ide-a-code-action-writes-only-what-is-already-determined) and on
the far side of the boundary the first editor slice draws.

A round trip asserts it: offered on a literal-initialized annotation, absent on a `Core\Json::decode`
initializer, and the file it produces still checks clean.

**Built:** *Narrow the type*, a `refactor.rewrite` action (`crates/nvs-lsp/src/narrow.rs`). It is offered
on the annotation of a local declaration, at any depth of statements and method bodies. A property's
default, a parameter's and a declaration inside a closure are not offered. The type comes from the
synthesis `var` runs: the document is analysed with `var` in place of the annotation, and the checker
records the literal's type there (`ExprTypeTable::literal_type`), the union of a literal it refuses
included. `nvs_types::narrow` widens and prints it. The round trip is
`a_narrowed_annotation_checks_as_before_and_is_not_offered_again` in `crates/nvs-lsp/tests/actions.rs`.

**Declined:**
- **A hint-severity diagnostic saying an annotation could be narrower.** It makes the checker say
  something new, and every deliberate `array<mixed>` would then need suppressing. That is every one
  that holds input.

<sub>See also [`ide/narrowest-means-narrowest-base-type`](ide.md#ide-narrowest-means-narrowest-base-type), [`ide/the-action-answers-from-the-literal-or-not-at-all`](ide.md#ide-the-action-answers-from-the-literal-or-not-at-all), [`ide/narrowing-is-a-diff-never-a-save-time-fix`](ide.md#ide-narrowing-is-a-diff-never-a-save-time-fix), [`ide/a-code-action-writes-only-what-is-already-determined`](ide.md#ide-a-code-action-writes-only-what-is-already-determined), [`types/arrays`](types.md#types-arrays), [`types/var-inference`](types.md#types-var-inference), [`ide/one-grammar-one-tree`](ide.md#ide-one-grammar-one-tree).</sub>

<a id="ide-narrowest-means-narrowest-base-type"></a>

## The synthesized element type is the canonical union of the elements' base types, recursed through nested literals and bounded at depth 32

`rule:ide/narrowest-means-narrowest-base-type`

The synthesized element type is the canonical union of the element types, **each widened to its base**:
the same widening [`types/single-value-types`](types.md#types-single-value-types) already performs at a placement, and the same union
canonicalisation the type table uses everywhere. So `['retry' => 1, 'depth' => 3]` yields `array<int>`
and never `array<1|3>`, which would be narrower and would refuse the next write made to it. An enum case
widens to its enum by the same call.

- A nested literal recurses, which is where the whole value of the action is: `array<array<array<float>>>`
  from one keystroke.
- `[]` already has type `array<never>`, which satisfies every `array<T>`, so there is nothing to offer and
  the action does not appear.
- The walk inherits the depth-32 descriptor bound of [`types/arrays`](types.md#types-arrays): past it the action declines
  rather than proposing a type the checker would then refuse.
- The action offers only a type that renders back to a spelling a developer could have written, because
  the edit it makes is source text a human reads in a diff.

The unit tests are the list: a homogeneous nest at three levels, a heterogeneous literal producing a
canonical union, an integer literal widening to `int`, an enum case widening to its enum, `[]` yielding no
offer, a `mixed` element yielding no offer, and a literal past depth 32 yielding no offer.

**Built:** `nvs_types::narrow::narrowest` widens the type the synthesis gave the literal and declines the
cases above, and `nvs_types::narrow::written` prints it, `?T` for a union of one type and `null`. A type
no annotation is written as declines too: a shape, an intersection, a `property<T>` key, a `string<K>`
and a callable signature. The unit tests are in `crates/nvs-types/src/narrow.rs`.

**Declined:**
- **The true narrowest type, literals included.** `array<1|3>` is narrower and correct, and it refuses
  the next write the developer makes. An action whose type its user must widen at once is worse than no
  action.

<sub>See also [`ide/narrow-an-annotation-to-its-literal`](ide.md#ide-narrow-an-annotation-to-its-literal), [`types/single-value-types`](types.md#types-single-value-types), [`types/enum-case-type`](types.md#types-enum-case-type), [`types/unions-and-mixed`](types.md#types-unions-and-mixed), [`types/arrays`](types.md#types-arrays).</sub>

<a id="ide-the-action-answers-from-the-literal-or-not-at-all"></a>

## The narrowing action answers from a literal in the same file, or it is not offered: no literal, a `mixed` element, or a no-op each hides it

`rule:ide/the-action-answers-from-the-literal-or-not-at-all`

Three refusals, and each is a soundness question rather than a difficulty one.

**No literal, no action.** `array<mixed> $body = Core\Json::decode($raw);` gets nothing. Neither does a
`Core\Request::query()`, a `Core\Script::args()` or any other value that arrives from outside — those are
`array<mixed>` on purpose ([`types/unions-and-mixed`](types.md#types-unions-and-mixed), [`statements/no-host-populated-variables`](statements.md#statements-no-host-populated-variables)).
The shape of one payload someone looked at does not bound the next request's, and narrowing there would
convert a runtime check into a compile-time assumption that is not true. This is security, not
ergonomics, and a developer may not point the action at such a value on the grounds that they know their
data.

**A `mixed` element poisons the answer, and a no-op is not offered.** An element whose own type is
`mixed` — including a spread of one — makes the union `mixed`, so the synthesis yields `array<mixed>` and
the action stays hidden rather than proposing the annotation that is already written.

**Everything else is answerable**, and that is a property of the language rather than of the
implementation: because every binding site declares a type, an element that is a variable or a call has a
type the checker already holds. Nothing in this action is guessed.

Narrowing from writes made *after* the declaration is not offered: it needs the join over every write
reaching the declaration and a generator that picks between answers, which
[`ide/a-code-action-writes-only-what-is-already-determined`](ide.md#ide-a-code-action-writes-only-what-is-already-determined) refuses. The cost half of that
objection goes away if the reference index of [`ide/five-features-are-one-reference-index`](ide.md#ide-five-features-are-one-reference-index) comes
to answer every write reaching a declaration; the choice half remains.

**Built:** `narrowing_is_not_offered_without_a_literal_that_states_the_type` in
`crates/nvs-lsp/tests/actions.rs` holds a decoded value, an empty literal at the top and nested, and a
`mixed` element to no offer. An initializer that is not an array literal is never asked about, so a
value from another file has no answer to give.

<sub>See also [`ide/narrow-an-annotation-to-its-literal`](ide.md#ide-narrow-an-annotation-to-its-literal), [`types/unions-and-mixed`](types.md#types-unions-and-mixed), [`statements/no-host-populated-variables`](statements.md#statements-no-host-populated-variables), [`security/tainted-sources`](security.md#security-tainted-sources).</sub>

<a id="ide-no-compile-path-calls-the-synthesis"></a>

## The synthesis is one function in `nvs-types`, called only where `var` types a bare array literal, and a union it finds is never attached to a binding

`rule:ide/no-compile-path-calls-the-synthesis`

The synthesis is a single function in `nvs-types` — a sibling of `check_array_literal`, not a change to
it — that types an array literal from its elements: `array<T>` when every element has the one type `T`,
and otherwise the reason it has none — two or more types with their canonical union, an empty literal,
or an element that could not be typed. It lives in the checker's crate rather than the editor's because
putting it beside the editor would mean a second implementation of union canonicalisation and literal
widening outside the type system that owns both, and the two would drift. The type table is the one home
for what a type is; the editor asks it a question.

**One compile path calls it, and only for a literal of one type.** `var`'s arm, for a bare literal
initializer, and the `foreach` subject under a `var` value binding are its two callers
([`types/var-inference`](types.md#types-var-inference)). Everywhere else `check_array_literal` still returns `array<mixed>` where it
has no expectation, so a literal written against a type stays checked against it ([`types/arrays`](types.md#types-arrays)),
and every other no-expectation position — an `echo` argument, a bare expression statement — types as it
did. A guard test counts the callers, so "no other position changed" is checkable rather than argued.

**A union is never attached to a binding.** Where the elements have two types the function returns the
union, and `var` refuses the literal and prints that union in its help line, for a person to write. The
editor action that narrows an annotation offers the same union as text in the file, read in a diff and
approved by a person ([`ide/narrow-an-annotation-to-its-literal`](ide.md#ide-narrow-an-annotation-to-its-literal)). A type only `var` held would be
visible nowhere, which is how a program acquires a type nobody chose. A literal of one type has no such
choice in it: the type is the one its elements state, so `var` takes it.

**Declined:**
- **`check_array_literal` returning the synthesized type wherever it has no expectation.** It is one
  line, and it is a language change: `echo` arguments and bare expression statements would retype, a
  heterogeneous literal under `var` would take a union nobody wrote, and [`types/arrays`](types.md#types-arrays)' checked
  literal would stop being checked.

<sub>See also [`types/var-inference`](types.md#types-var-inference), [`types/arrays`](types.md#types-arrays), [`ide/narrow-an-annotation-to-its-literal`](ide.md#ide-narrow-an-annotation-to-its-literal).</sub>

<a id="ide-narrowing-is-a-diff-never-a-save-time-fix"></a>

## The narrowing action is never registered under `source.fixAll.nvs` and never chases the call sites it affects, because it breaks writes it cannot see

`rule:ide/narrowing-is-a-diff-never-a-save-time-fix`

Narrowing a declaration is not a local edit, because [`types/arrays`](types.md#types-arrays)' element type is enforced on
every **write**: a binding that was an `array<mixed>` and is now an `array<array<int>>` refuses the
`$a[] = "x"` and the `$a = $wider;` that the wider annotation admitted, each of them a line the action
did not touch. Reading it is what stays safe — the narrowed array still satisfies every wider parameter
it reached before, that being the covariant direction — so what the action can break is exactly the
writes, and it cannot see them from the declaration. Two rules follow.

**The action is never registered under `source.fixAll.nvs`.** The casing fix and the legacy-cast fix
compose with format-on-save because their edit cannot break another line. This one can, so it is invoked,
previewed and approved like the generators beside it. A client test asserts it is absent from the
`source.fixAll.nvs` set, so a format-on-save never applies it.

**It does not chase the call sites it affects.** Repairing them means choosing between an `as` at the
call, a wider parameter and a narrower one — a refactoring with a decision in it, which
[`ide/a-code-action-writes-only-what-is-already-determined`](ide.md#ide-a-code-action-writes-only-what-is-already-determined) refuses to let a light bulb make.

The request path gets faster where the action is used, which is the point: a narrowed array leaves the
generic helper path for the typed one, and its element writes become compile errors instead of runtime
throws. Nothing is spent per request, and no memory beyond one more interned descriptor where the program
did not already have that type.

**Built:** the action is a `refactor.rewrite` appended only to a quick-fix answer
(`crates/nvs-lsp/src/actions.rs`), and the round trip in `crates/nvs-lsp/tests/actions.rs` asks for
`source.fixAll.nvs` and is answered nothing. The writes it cannot see from the declaration are seen by
the analysis it runs before the offer: the document with the edit applied must report exactly the
diagnostics it reports now, so a later `$a[] = "x"` that the narrower type refuses hides the action.

<sub>See also [`ide/narrow-an-annotation-to-its-literal`](ide.md#ide-narrow-an-annotation-to-its-literal), [`ide/a-code-action-writes-only-what-is-already-determined`](ide.md#ide-a-code-action-writes-only-what-is-already-determined), [`types/arrays`](types.md#types-arrays), [`types/conversion`](types.md#types-conversion), [`tooling/fmt-is-never-a-diagnostic`](tooling.md#tooling-fmt-is-never-a-diagnostic), [`ide/every-feature-is-staged-behind-its-dependency`](ide.md#ide-every-feature-is-staged-behind-its-dependency).</sub>

<a id="ide-highlighting-is-two-layers"></a>

## Syntax highlighting is a TextMate grammar and a semantic-token provider, each with its own test, and each must cover what makes Novis not PHP

`rule:ide/highlighting-is-two-layers`

"Colour" is two deliverables because the two layers fail differently: the grammar has to be right before
the server has started, and the server has to be right about things a regex cannot see.

**Layer one, the TextMate grammar** (`editors/vscode/syntaxes/nvs.tmLanguage.json`), is what a file looks
like the instant it opens. It must cover, because a grammar borrowed from another language gets each one
wrong: the dual-mode lexer's openers `<?nvs`, `<?php`, `<?=` and `?>`, with inline HTML outside them
highlighted as HTML; heredoc and nowdoc, with interpolation only in the former; type annotations everywhere
the grammar allows one, including the inline shape `{x: int}` ([`types/object-top`](types.md#types-object-top)); the qualifiers
`tainted` and `secret`, and `decimal` as a scalar keyword ([`types/decimal`](types.md#types-decimal)); `spawn`, `spawn script`,
`autoload`, `type`, `by`-delegation, property hooks and their `get`/`set` bodies; durations
([`types/duration`](types.md#types-duration)); `#[...]` attributes distinguished from a `#` comment, with the attribute's
class as a type and each named argument as a property; every name after `extends` or `implements`
and the path of an import, which the word before each says is a type; the class before `::`, which
is a type too; a member that is called, and every lowercase name after `::`, which the parser reads
as a method ([`expressions/method-reference`](expressions.md#expressions-method-reference)); and nothing Novis
rejects ([`ide/rejected-syntax-gets-no-colour`](ide.md#ide-rejected-syntax-gets-no-colour)). The grammar also colours every name a theme
needs before the server answers: layer two adds what it resolves, and a theme that discards semantic
tokens would otherwise show those names as body text ([`ide/novis-ships-names-not-colours`](ide.md#ide-novis-ships-names-not-colours)). Its test needs no editor: `vscode-textmate` plus
`vscode-oniguruma` tokenize a fixture and a snapshot freezes the scope of every span.

**Layer two, semantic tokens**, is where a compiler colours what a regex cannot know
([`ide/semantic-tokens-carry-the-qualifiers`](ide.md#ide-semantic-tokens-carry-the-qualifiers)). Its test is a `.lspt` case per token type, plus the
extension-host run confirming the client's legend matches the server's.

<sub>See also [`ide/rejected-syntax-gets-no-colour`](ide.md#ide-rejected-syntax-gets-no-colour), [`ide/semantic-tokens-carry-the-qualifiers`](ide.md#ide-semantic-tokens-carry-the-qualifiers), [`ide/novis-ships-names-not-colours`](ide.md#ide-novis-ships-names-not-colours), [`ide/case-files-have-their-own-grammar`](ide.md#ide-case-files-have-their-own-grammar), [`types/object-top`](types.md#types-object-top), [`types/duration`](types.md#types-duration), [`types/decimal`](types.md#types-decimal), [`tooling/doc-comment-is-three-slashes`](tooling.md#tooling-doc-comment-is-three-slashes).</sub>

<a id="ide-rejected-syntax-gets-no-colour"></a>

## Nothing Novis rejects is coloured as though it were valid

`rule:ide/rejected-syntax-gets-no-colour`

Nothing Novis rejects may be coloured as though it were valid. `===` and `!==` are not operators
([`expressions/one-equality-operator`](expressions.md#expressions-one-equality-operator)), `(int)$x` is not a cast ([`types/no-legacy-cast`](types.md#types-no-legacy-cast)), `|>` is
not a call of a callable on its right ([`expressions/pipeline-substitution`](expressions.md#expressions-pipeline-substitution)), and the alternative colon syntax
(`if (...): ... endif;`) is not syntax at all.

A grammar that colours these confirms a mistake in the editor before the server contradicts it, which is
worse than no colour. `editors/vscode/test/grammar/rejected.test.ts` asserts each of these receives no
scope that reads as valid, and the grammar suite beside it holds the positive cases — a `#[Route]`
attribute that is not a comment, a nowdoc that does not interpolate, inline HTML outside `<?nvs`.

<sub>See also [`ide/highlighting-is-two-layers`](ide.md#ide-highlighting-is-two-layers), [`expressions/one-equality-operator`](expressions.md#expressions-one-equality-operator), [`types/no-legacy-cast`](types.md#types-no-legacy-cast), [`expressions/pipeline-substitution`](expressions.md#expressions-pipeline-substitution).</sub>

<a id="ide-semantic-tokens-carry-the-qualifiers"></a>

## Semantic tokens use LSP's standard types plus two modifiers of Novis's own, `tainted` and `secret`, and the client's legend must equal the server's

`rule:ide/semantic-tokens-carry-the-qualifiers`

The token types the server emits are each chosen because the grammar structurally cannot answer them:
`namespace`, `class` (with `defaultLibrary` for a `Core` class, so the standard library is visibly not
user code), `interface`, `enum`, `enumMember`, `type` (an alias), `method`, `property`, `parameter`,
`variable`, `typeParameter` — and two modifiers of Novis's own, **`tainted` and `secret`**, so a qualified
value is visibly qualified at every use site rather than only where it was declared.

That pair is why this layer is part of the editor's minimum: [`security/tainted-qualifier`](security.md#security-tainted-qualifier)'s and
[`security/secret-qualifier`](security.md#security-secret-qualifier)'s whole model is that a value carries a qualifier through the program, and
an editor that shows it is the cheapest teaching surface the language has. "The qualifier is visible" is
verified as "the token carries the modifier", never as a colour.

The name in front of a `::` is coloured as what it resolved to — `enum` before a case, `class` before
a constant, a static call or a static property — carrying `defaultLibrary` for a `Core` enum exactly as
for a `Core` class. An attribute's name is a `type` token, since it names the shape its payload
satisfies, with `defaultLibrary` for a compiler attribute; its payload is coloured as the expressions
it holds, so `Core\Http\Method::Get` inside `#[...]` reads as it does in a body.

The legend the client registers must equal the legend the server declares. A mismatch silently colours
everything one token type off, which no unit test on either side alone can see, so the extension-host run
proves it.

**Declined:**
- **The TextMate grammar alone, with semantic tokens left for later.** A regex grammar cannot produce the
  qualifier modifiers at any price, and they are the reason this layer exists.

<sub>See also [`ide/highlighting-is-two-layers`](ide.md#ide-highlighting-is-two-layers), [`ide/novis-ships-names-not-colours`](ide.md#ide-novis-ships-names-not-colours), [`security/tainted-qualifier`](security.md#security-tainted-qualifier), [`security/secret-qualifier`](security.md#security-secret-qualifier), [`ide/tainted-has-no-default-decoration`](ide.md#ide-tainted-has-no-default-decoration).</sub>

<a id="ide-novis-ships-names-not-colours"></a>

## Both layers ship standard names: every scope is on the TextMate allowlist, every token type is in LSP's legend, and the extension sets a colour only where the user picks one

`rule:ide/novis-ships-names-not-colours`

Colour is the user's theme's to decide. Both layers ship *names*, and a theme styles only the names it
already recognises, which makes naming the whole of the work and the whole of the risk.

Every scope the TextMate grammar emits comes from the standard TextMate vocabulary, suffixed `.nvs` —
`keyword.control.nvs`, `storage.type.nvs`, `entity.name.type.class.nvs`, `string.quoted.double.nvs`. An
invented name like `keyword.nvs.spawn` is matched by no theme, so the construct renders as unstyled body
text: technically correct and visibly broken. The grammar snapshot test asserts every scope it produces is
on an allowlist of standard names, so a novel one fails in CI rather than in somebody's editor.

Every semantic token type comes from LSP's standard legend. The two modifiers Novis adds are by definition
not in it, so the extension declares `semanticTokenScopes`, mapping each to a standard TextMate scope a
theme already styles: `*.tainted` to `markup.underline` and `*.secret` to `emphasis`. Both scopes carry a
font style and no colour in the themes VS Code ships, and VS Code resolves each style property from the
rule that sets it, so a qualified variable is underlined or italic and keeps its variable colour. A theme
with no rule for either scope draws the plain token type. The extension ships no `configurationDefaults`
for `editor.tokenColorCustomizations` or
`editor.semanticTokenColorCustomizations`: whatever a `tainted` value ought to look like is not Novis's
call to make in someone else's editor, which is also what
[`ide/tainted-has-no-default-decoration`](ide.md#ide-tainted-has-no-default-decoration) applies.

Colour Novis does choose reaches an editor only when the user picks it, in one of two ways. Both exist
because a popular theme can draw a type and a method in two near-identical shades, and the names alone
cannot fix that. The extension bundles two themes, `Novis Dark` and `Novis Light`, which style the
standard scopes and token types of every language and are never selected for the user. The
`nvs.highlighting.distinctNames` setting, off by default, keeps the user's theme: turned on, it writes
a type's and a method's colour as `:nvs` rules into the user's
`editor.semanticTokenColorCustomizations`, under the theme showing and under each theme switched to
later, and turned off it removes every rule whose value is still the one it wrote. Both use the one
palette in `editors/vscode/src/colours.ts`. The setting's description says both, with a `command:`
link that switches to the bundled theme, because the Settings editor runs such a link in one click.

The extension does turn semantic highlighting on for `.nvs` documents, with the `configurationDefaults`
entry `"[nvs]": { "editor.semanticHighlighting.enabled": true }`. VS Code's own default,
`configuredByTheme`, lets a theme that sets `"semanticHighlighting": false` discard every semantic
token, and many popular themes set it. Under such a theme layer two is gone: an attribute's class, a
named argument and a resolved type show as body text, and the `tainted` underline and the `secret`
emphasis never appear. Turning the setting on ships names and no colour. Without
`semanticTokenColors` of its own, a theme colours each semantic token through the TextMate scope VS
Code maps its type to, so the theme still decides every colour. The setting is read per language, so
no other language's highlighting changes, and a user's own `[nvs]` setting wins over the default.

**Declined:**

- **Leaving the setting to the theme.** The cost is the whole of layer two under every theme that
  opts out, and the user who meets it sees a half-coloured file with no hint of the cause.
- **Writing the rules as a default, or for every theme at once.** A default is a colour the user did
  not pick, and one palette cannot suit both a light and a dark theme, so the rules go under one
  theme's block, in the shade that theme is drawn in.

**Built:** the grammar's allowlist test (`editors/vscode/test/grammar/allowlist.test.ts`), the standard
legend, the `semanticTokenScopes` contribution, the semantic highlighting default, no colour defaults,
the two bundled themes and the `nvs.highlighting.distinctNames` setting in
`editors/vscode/package.json`; `editors/vscode/test/contributions/contributions.test.ts` asserts all
but the first two, and `editors/vscode/test/client/colours.test.ts` asserts what the setting writes and
removes.

<sub>See also [`ide/highlighting-is-two-layers`](ide.md#ide-highlighting-is-two-layers), [`ide/semantic-tokens-carry-the-qualifiers`](ide.md#ide-semantic-tokens-carry-the-qualifiers), [`ide/tainted-has-no-default-decoration`](ide.md#ide-tainted-has-no-default-decoration).</sub>

<a id="ide-five-features-are-one-reference-index"></a>

## Find-references, occurrence highlight, CodeLens, type hierarchy and unused-member dimming are five queries against one workspace index

`rule:ide/five-features-are-one-reference-index`

`nvs-lsp` builds one workspace symbol index, and five features are each one query against it — none
gets a walk of its own. `textDocument/references` is the index's read side, and it lists each `use` line
that imports the name among its uses; the CodeLens count leaves those lines out, because an import brings
a name into scope and uses nothing. `textDocument/documentHighlight`
is the same query narrowed to the open file, which is why it reads the index rather than the open
document alone: it needs resolution applied to every occurrence, not to one. CodeLens above a declaration shows
the reference count, a type's implementors, and the methods a method overrides and is overridden by; it is
gated on `nvs.codeLens.enable` (default `true`), because a lens is a request per visible declaration and a
large file is where it is least welcome. A click on a lens lists the places it counts. The lens carries
`nvs.showLocations` with the document, its position and those places, and only for a client that names
that id in `capabilities.experimental.commands`; every other client gets a label. The VS Code client
registers the id and opens the editor's reference view. The id is frozen like a contributed command, and
the places cost one file load per file that holds one, per lens request. `textDocument/typeHierarchy` shows supertypes and subtypes,
including [`classes/interface-default-methods`](classes.md#classes-interface-default-methods) and [`classes/delegation-by-property`](classes.md#classes-delegation-by-property), which is
where a reader most needs to see the shape rather than reconstruct it.

The fifth is **unused-member dimming**: a private member or constant with no reference anywhere in
the index is a diagnostic carrying LSP's `Unnecessary` tag, rendered as dimming rather than a squiggle.
An unused `use` line is not dimmed here: it is the `W1026` warning of
[`statements/an-unused-use-is-a-warning`](statements.md#statements-an-unused-use-is-a-warning), which carries the same tag.
It is only correct at workspace scope — a symbol unused in the open buffer is not unused — so it is
silent under the default of [`ide/check-scope-defaults-to-the-workspace`](ide.md#ide-check-scope-defaults-to-the-workspace) rather than wrong.

The index is also the **call graph**. Each occurrence records the method whose body it is written in,
so an occurrence that resolved to a method is an edge from that method to it. Beside the occurrences,
each file records two more lists. One holds each `Core\Test::request` whose literal method and path
the route table matched, as an edge to the route's handler. The other holds each call the graph does
not follow: a method taken as a callable value, and a call by name the checker did not resolve. A
method's declaration records the routes it handles and whether it is a `#[Test]` method.
`nvs_lsp::reach` walks these edges backwards for
[`ide/used-by-counts-the-routes-and-tests-that-reach-a-method`](ide.md#ide-used-by-counts-the-routes-and-tests-that-reach-a-method), and `textDocument/callHierarchy`
reads the same edges rather than a second index ([`ide/the-request-set-is-closed`](ide.md#ide-the-request-set-is-closed)). The graph
costs one method name per occurrence and two short lists per file, for as long as the file is indexed.

One more reader reads the same index and is not a reference feature: `nvs/fileKinds`
([`ide/a-file-shows-what-it-declares`](ide.md#ide-a-file-shows-what-it-declares)) lists the files that declare one type, from the kind the index
recorded as it read each file. It asks what a file declares rather than where a name is used, and it
builds no walk of its own either.

`workspace/symbol` reads it too: `SymbolIndex::matching` returns every declaration whose own name (a
type's last segment, or a member without a property's `$`) contains the query, upper and lower case
alike. It searches the declarations the index already holds, so it adds no store and no walk.

The same index answers a question asked by name. `nvs_lsp::query` holds the readers that take a
fully-qualified name instead of a cursor, and the editor feature that asks the same question calls the
same function: `textDocument/references` and `textDocument/implementation` read the cursor's name and
call `query`. A caller outside the server, such as `nvs code`, gets a `Workspace` from `server.rs`, which
builds the index for one question and drops it with the answer.

The structure is one constructor, `SymbolIndex::build` in `crates/nvs-lsp/src/index.rs`, and all seven
readers read what it built. The server keeps one warm index; a `.lspt` case and `nvs code` call the
same constructor for one question each. Five features that would each walk the workspace cost one walk between them, and the
warm index is what keeps references and highlight inside [`ide/a-full-reanalysis-stays-under-a-bound`](ide.md#ide-a-full-reanalysis-stays-under-a-bound).

- **Memory:** the index holds one entry per file the workspace's analyses reached, for the life of the
  server process. It is bounded by the tree `nvs.check.scope` selects and released by the invalidation a
  keystroke triggers. It is spent in the editor process and never on the request path.

**Declined:**
- **An index scoped to one `require` graph.** Four readers would work, but unused-member dimming is only
  correct at workspace scope. It would also make the scope a property of the index rather than of the
  query, so the fifth reader would need a second construction site.

<sub>See also [`ide/check-scope-defaults-to-the-workspace`](ide.md#ide-check-scope-defaults-to-the-workspace), [`classes/no-traits`](classes.md#classes-no-traits), [`classes/interface-default-methods`](classes.md#classes-interface-default-methods), [`classes/delegation-by-property`](classes.md#classes-delegation-by-property), [`ide/contributions-are-frozen-and-only-ever-added`](ide.md#ide-contributions-are-frozen-and-only-ever-added), [`ide/every-feature-is-staged-behind-its-dependency`](ide.md#ide-every-feature-is-staged-behind-its-dependency).</sub>

<a id="ide-used-by-counts-the-routes-and-tests-that-reach-a-method"></a>

## A method's "used by" lens counts the routes whose handlers reach it through resolved calls and the tests the last coverage run saw reach it, and a click runs exactly those tests

`rule:ide/used-by-counts-the-routes-and-tests-that-reach-a-method`

Above a method, a code lens says "used by N routes, M tests". A click runs exactly the tests it
counted, through the Test Explorer's own filtered run
([`ide/the-test-tree-is-discovered-and-run-through-the-cli`](ide.md#ide-the-test-tree-is-discovered-and-run-through-the-cli)).

**A route counts through the call graph.** A route counts when its handler reaches the method through a
chain of calls the checker resolved, the handler itself as the first link. The chain is a call graph
read off the one reference index ([`ide/five-features-are-one-reference-index`](ide.md#ide-five-features-are-one-reference-index)). Each occurrence
records the function or method it is written in, so an occurrence that resolved to a method is an edge
from that function to it. The graph is the index read one more way, never a second walk of the
workspace. Reach walks callers backwards from the method and visits each function once, so a recursive
chain ends.

**A test counts through the last coverage run, and through the call graph where there is none.** The
user decided this. When the Coverage run profile has run, its JSON report lists the lines each test
reached ([`testing/report-formats`](testing.md#testing-report-formats), [`testing/coverage-report`](testing.md#testing-coverage-report)), and a test counts when it
reached a line of the method. That count is exact for the run it came from. Where no report exists,
a test counts when its `#[Test]` method reaches the method through the call graph, or when it calls
`Core\Test::request` with a literal method and path that the compiled route table matches to a route
that counts ([`testing/in-process-request`](testing.md#testing-in-process-request)), and the lens marks the test count "static". The match
is the server's own matcher, so the lens and the server never disagree about which handler answers a
path. A path built at run time is not matched.

A call the checker did not resolve to one method is not followed: a call through a `callable` value,
and a call by name on a `mixed` receiver. Where either could reach the method, the lens puts "at
least" before a count read off the graph. That is the case when the method is taken as a callable
value anywhere in the workspace, or when a call on a `mixed` receiver names a method of the same name.
A call resolved to a method that the reached method overrides is not followed either, because which
of the two runs is decided at run time; where such a call exists, the count is "at least" too.
A count read off the graph is never too high: everything counted reaches the method. A call written
in a closure counts as a call from the method that writes the closure, which is where a reader looks
for it.

The route count and a static test count are read from the index, so they are current after every edit.
A test count from a report is as old as its run, and the next coverage run refreshes it. The lens is
gated on `nvs.codeLens.enable` with the other lenses.

**The client keeps the reports, one per program.** The VS Code client writes the JSON report of each
program's last coverage run into a directory of its own storage, with every file name made absolute,
and names that directory in `initialize`'s `coverage.dir`, as it names `stubs.dir`. A report applies
to a file one of its tests reached. Where none did, the count is the call graph's and says "static". A
test the index no longer declares is not counted. **A method that no route and no test reaches has no
"used by" lens**, for the reason a hierarchy lens is written only where it has something to say.
**Neither has a `#[Test]` method**: it would count 0 routes and the one test that is itself, and the
Test Explorer's run button beside it already runs it. For the same reason, a `#[Test]` method and the
class that declares it have a reference count only when it is above 0. The runner finds both by the
attribute, so "no references" would be true of every test. A click carries `nvs.runTests` with the
tests as `Class::method`, for a client that names that command.

- **Memory:** one function name per occurrence in the index, held in the editor process for the
  index's life, and the newest report's per-test lines while the server holds it. Each lens request
  allocates its visited set and frees it with the answer. Nothing at compile time for running, and
  nothing at run time.

**Declined:**
- **Counting tests by the call graph alone.** A test that reaches the method only through a `callable`
  or a path built at run time would never count, and a test that names the method on a branch it never
  takes would. The coverage run already records what each test reached.
- **Following a call through a `callable` value or a `mixed` receiver.** Its target is known only at
  run time, so a count through it is a guess. "at least" says where the count may be low.

<sub>See also [`ide/five-features-are-one-reference-index`](ide.md#ide-five-features-are-one-reference-index), [`routing/routes-are-compiled-not-registered`](routing.md#routing-routes-are-compiled-not-registered), [`testing/in-process-request`](testing.md#testing-in-process-request), [`testing/report-formats`](testing.md#testing-report-formats), [`testing/coverage-report`](testing.md#testing-coverage-report), [`ide/the-test-tree-is-discovered-and-run-through-the-cli`](ide.md#ide-the-test-tree-is-discovered-and-run-through-the-cli), [`ide/the-request-set-is-closed`](ide.md#ide-the-request-set-is-closed).</sub>

<a id="ide-a-route-hover-shows-the-programs-grants"></a>

## Hovering a route shows what the program's grants allow, labelled as that program's and read from the `nvs.toml` that `nvs check` reads in that directory

`rule:ide/a-route-hover-shows-the-programs-grants`

Hovering a `#[Route]` attribute, or the name of the method it is on, shows what the program's grants
allow: the files it may read and write, the hosts it may connect to, the databases it may open, the
processes it may run, and every other grant by its name, each with its scope. The hover's first line
names the `nvs.toml` it read and says that the grants are the program's. The attribute keeps its own
card above the grants; the method's name answers the grants alone.

The grants are the configuration snapshot for the hovered file, resolved the way `nvs check` resolves
it when run in that directory, through the same reader the extension set uses
(`nvs_lsp::document::program_tree`). Every capability of the closed roster is a line: what the
snapshot writes for it, or its default for server work marked `(default)` where it writes nothing. A
default that grants nothing is not a line, and one closing sentence says no other grant is given.
Nothing is inferred from the code, so the hover is exactly as deep as the grant table the runtime
enforces ([`security/capability-question-is-grant-and-scope`](security.md#security-capability-question-is-grant-and-scope)). An edit to the grants changes the
hover with no edit to the source, because the tree is resolved again for each hover, as the extension
set is: a cached tree would outlive an edit to `nvs.toml`. With no `nvs.toml`, the hover says that
none was found and lists the default policy. A tree that does not load is named, with no grants, and
`nvs check` reports why.

A path inside the hovered file's directory is written relative to it, and any other path whole. The
text is `nvs_lsp::grants::of_program`'s.

A grant belongs to a program, never to a route, so the hover never presents it as the route's.
Diagnostics are answered with no grants (`nvs_lsp::document::analyse_file`'s type phase), because a
diagnostic sits on a line of code and cannot say which configuration it came from. A hover can, in its
first line, so the reader always sees which file answered.

- **Memory:** nothing at compile time for running and nothing at run time. A hover reads the
  configuration tree once and frees it with the answer.

**Declined:**
- **Narrowing the grants to what one route's handler calls.** It would be a guess from the code at
  what the program may do, and the runtime checks the program's grant, not the guess.

<sub>See also [`security/capability-question-is-grant-and-scope`](security.md#security-capability-question-is-grant-and-scope), [`ide/the-request-set-is-closed`](ide.md#ide-the-request-set-is-closed), [`routing/routes-are-compiled-not-registered`](routing.md#routing-routes-are-compiled-not-registered).</sub>

<a id="ide-a-query-lens-shows-what-one-recorded-request-ran-at-a-site"></a>

## Above each query call, a lens shows what the newest recorded request that reached it ran there: the count, the total and the slowest time, and whether one statement repeated

`rule:ide/a-query-lens-shows-what-one-recorded-request-ran-at-a-site`

With `[debug] store` on, each `Core\Db` call that sends a statement gets a code lens read from the debug
service's index ([`testing/the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking`](testing.md#testing-the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking)). It describes the
newest recorded request whose trace reached that site: how many statements ran there, their total time
and the slowest one. When one statement text ran at the site more than once in that request, the lens
says it repeated and how many times, which is the N+1 pattern a query inside a loop makes. A click
opens that request in the viewer, at the `[debug] listen` address of the program's configuration
tree, through the editor's own `vscode.open` command, which a client names in
`capabilities.experimental.commands` as it names the others. The server sends no command to a client
that did not name it, and the lens is then a title alone.

A query is grouped by its call site, the file, line and file hash its traced span records
([`observability/a-query-span-names-its-call-site`](observability.md#observability-a-query-span-names-its-call-site)), never by its text. So the figures are a few
numbers per site a request reached, however many times a loop ran the query, which is
[`testing/debug-surface`](testing.md#testing-debug-surface)'s argument for line counters. The debug index looks a site up on an
index of its own over the hash and the line. The statement is shown as written, its placeholders
still placeholders: no parameter value is recorded or shown
([`observability/a-query-is-a-trace-event`](observability.md#observability-a-query-is-a-trace-event)).

Each site carries the hash of its file's text when the program was compiled, and a record whose hash is
not the hash of the text the editor holds is not shown, so an unsaved edit hides the lens until a
request runs the new text. A lens never sits on a line that ran something else.

The server opens the index read-only, from the data folder, and makes no network request. An index
that is absent, or that the service holds locked, gives no lens and no error.

- **Memory:** in the editor process, a few numbers per query site per lens request, freed with the
  answer, and the start and end of each query call in the reference index. In the spool and the
  index, one file, line and hash per traced query and one entry of the site index, under the
  service's byte cap.

**Declined:**
- **One parameter set kept per site.** No query span holds a parameter value, and a parameter is
  where request input and secrets are.
- **Variable values shown inline from recorded requests.** Recording values grows with every iteration
  and every request. A conditional breakpoint or a logpoint in `nvs dap` answers the same question on
  demand.
- **Picking the request in the viewer.** It needs state shared between the viewer and the editor. The
  newest request that reached the site is the one a developer just sent.

<sub>See also [`observability/a-query-span-names-its-call-site`](observability.md#observability-a-query-span-names-its-call-site), [`observability/a-query-is-a-trace-event`](observability.md#observability-a-query-is-a-trace-event), [`testing/the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking`](testing.md#testing-the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking), [`testing/debug-surface`](testing.md#testing-debug-surface), [`ide/the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has`](ide.md#ide-the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has).</sub>

<a id="ide-completion-offers-only-what-the-compiler-derived"></a>

## The editor completes a value only where the compiler already derives it for another reason or a completion file lists it, never from a framework's conventions, an annotation dialect or the network

`rule:ide/completion-offers-only-what-the-compiler-derived`

`nvs-lsp` contains no framework-specific module, no annotation dialect, no scan for a framework's
conventions and no directory-layout knowledge. It offers a **value** in a completion list only where the
compiler already derives that value for another reason, reaching it through the same table that other
reason uses, or where a completion file under a `.novis/completion/` folder lists it for the parameter
the cursor is at ([`ide/completion-files-offer-values-at-named-parameters`](ide.md#ide-completion-files-offer-values-at-named-parameters)). This is the whole of
Novis's answer to "framework support", and it is a closed rule, not a starting point.

What that admits: the methods that carry a `#[Route]`, offered first in a link's or a match
check's first argument, and their parameters, from the route table
[`routing/routes-are-compiled-not-registered`](routing.md#routing-routes-are-compiled-not-registered) builds while compiling — the same table
[`routing/link-target-and-params-are-checked`](routing.md#routing-link-target-and-params-are-checked) checks a link against; configuration directives in a
file named `nvs.toml` ([`ide/the-extension-claims-nvs-only`](ide.md#ide-the-extension-claims-nvs-only)), from the default file the binary ships,
which `bun nv directives --check-template` holds to the parser that refuses an unknown key
([`config/a-duplicate-key-is-an-error-and-so-is-an-unknown-one`](config.md#config-a-duplicate-key-is-an-error-and-so-is-an-unknown-one)), so completion, hover with type and
default, and "no such directive" are three readings of one registry, and `[[include]]`'s `path` and `dir`
complete as paths — scoped to the workspace's config tree, never to every TOML file; a `require` path,
an `autoload` root or `discover` glob, and a string argument at a parameter the registry or
`#[Core\Path]` marks as a path, which complete as the entries of the one directory the text before the
cursor reaches, read through the listing the compiler resolves a glob with; an `autoload` prefix, which
completes as the namespaces of the declarations the workspace index and the analysis already hold; the
string converted with `as class<T>`, which completes as the classes the program declares that are a
`T`, read through the hierarchy walk the checker answers that question with; a string argument at a
parameter the registry marks as a class name, which completes as the classes the program declares, and
as the ones that are a `Throwable` where the member expects an error; a string argument at a parameter
whose declared type is a set of allowed string values ([`types/single-value-types`](types.md#types-single-value-types)), which completes as
those values, read off the parameter types the checker records on the call it resolved; the string
converted with `as property<T>`, and a string argument at a parameter whose type takes a `property<T>`
beside a `string`, which complete as `T`'s public declared properties with their types, read off the set
the checker tests that conversion against ([`types/property-key`](types.md#types-property-key)); the field names of a compiler
attribute's payload, such as `#[Api]`'s, from the attribute's card, which is held to the roster the
checker reads the payload against; the security schemes the program declares with `#[Api\Scheme]`, at
an entry of an `#[Api]` `security` list, from the route table the checker holds each such name against
([`routing/a-security-scheme-is-declared-in-code`](routing.md#routing-a-security-scheme-is-declared-in-code)); every attribute's anonymous object, whose shape
is a declared type; and enum cases, members off a resolved receiver
and in-scope variables, which are the same rule and not an exception to it.

A path list is one directory: the text between the opening quote and the cursor is split at its last
separator, the part before it is joined to the declaring file's directory (the base `require` and
`autoload` resolve against) or replaces it when absolute, and that directory is listed through
`nvs_hir::autoload::entries_of`, so a name offered is one resolution would find. Names are offered as the
disk spells them ([`programs/path-case`](programs.md#programs-path-case)), a name starting with `.` is hidden, and an item replaces
only the segment after the last separator. A directory item writes a `/` and opens the list again. A
`require` offers directories and `.nvs` files, an `autoload` literal directories only, and a path
argument every file, since a path parameter takes a file of any kind. Nothing is offered once the
directory part holds a `*`. An `autoload` prefix offers namespaces from the workspace index as well as
the analysis, `Core` excluded, because a prefix usually maps code nothing loads yet. The string of `as
class<T>` offers each class and interface in the analysis that `nvs_hir::hierarchy::implements_interface`
says is a `T`, `T` included, and not a class only an autoload root could load, because the run-time
conversion compares whole names among the classes the program declares and cannot find that one either.
A name literal's item is a whole name replacing all the text after the opening quote: a `\` typed just
before the closing quote escapes it, so no list can be answered at that keystroke, and a whole name
never needs it. `Core\Test::assertThrows` is the one member whose class-name parameter expects an
error, named in a one-row table in `crate::arguments`, since the mark says only that the text is a class
name. A parameter whose type is a set of allowed string values completes them as items of kind
`value`, its `null` aside, and is offered a completion file's list beside them, merged by value; it gets
no warning for a literal outside the set, because the checker already rejects one.

A property name is an item of kind `property` with its declared type at the right. The checker records
the set for each class a `property<T>` names at an `as` conversion, and at a string literal argument for
a parameter whose type has a `property<T>` member, because the walk that makes the set needs the signature
table and the editor does not keep one. A parameter typed `property<T>|string` takes any string, so a
literal outside the set gets no warning there. A parameter typed `property<T>` alone, or `?property<T>`,
is offered the same names, because the checker converts a string literal there while compiling
([`types/property-key`](types.md#types-property-key)), and a wrong one is its own diagnostic. A parameter typed `propertyPath<T>`,
and a hole of a literal at a `string<K>` parameter or under `as string<K>`, is offered the names one
segment at a time, from the sets the checker records for each class the path reaches
([`ide/a-field-path-completes-one-segment-at-a-time`](ide.md#ide-a-field-path-completes-one-segment-at-a-time)). A hole of a `string<K>` whose `K` lists
string values is offered those values.

- **Memory:** one list of names and types per class a `property<T>` names or a path reaches, kept with
  the checker's table for the length of the analysis. Nothing at run time.

What it refuses has no subject rather than being declined: ORM columns (a codec's fields are declared
properties, already reached as members), and service-container, facade and view-name resolution (`Core`
has no container and no view layer, [`programs/no-first-party-framework`](programs.md#programs-no-first-party-framework)). A vendor annotation dialect is
refused outright as a second, unchecked description of the program's shape — the failure
[`routing/api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table`](routing.md#routing-api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table) refuses for API documents. A completion
file is not one: it describes values the compiler never holds, such as the keys of a dataset or the
names in an icon set, and never a class, a member or a type. It is data and is never run. And **the
language server makes no network request**: a lockfile on disk may be read, a remote index may not be
consulted.

A test, not review, enforces this: `nvs-lsp`'s completion sources are enumerated, and each must name a
table the compiler builds for another reason or the table the completion files were loaded into. No
completion source reads a directory or a file itself.

The text an item inserts comes from the same place: a `Core` member is inserted from the registry the
checker seeds its signatures from, so a suggestion never writes a call that then fails to resolve. An
editor that writes such a call is worse than one that offers nothing, because the developer cannot tell
the suggestion's mistake from their own.

The rule buys a stronger guarantee than framework-aware completion elsewhere gives. A route's
method completed from the compile-time route table is correct, where one recovered by scanning a conventions
directory is a good guess. Columns recovered from migrations, facades followed through a runtime
container and components found by directory convention are each a heuristic replacing a fact the
language does not make available; Novis makes those facts available, so the heuristic has nothing to
replace. Stating the rule as a property of where a value comes from keeps `nvs-lsp` free of
per-framework modules, which would otherwise arrive one framework at a time and never leave.

What it costs: a package whose route-like table is built while the program runs gets no completion for
it, and the answer is to make that table compile-time. An editor that talks to a third party while a
developer types is the same class of surprise [`http-server/allow-url-pins-the-address`](http-server.md#http-server-allow-url-pins-the-address) refuses for
a running program, which is why no completion source fetches anything.

**Declined:**
- **Framework support built from convention scans, an annotation dialect and a patch file** for what
  neither reaches. Each is a second description of a program's shape that nothing checks against the
  first.
- **A module for the first-party web framework inside `nvs-lsp`.** It would be the server's first
  special case, and a third-party package would then ask for the same treatment with no principle left
  to refuse it.
- **Package-name and version completion in the manifest, from a registry.** It needs a network request
  while the user types. A lockfile's resolved versions are on disk and may be shown.
- **PHP built-in names as candidates, each answered with its Novis destination.** The answer needs a
  table from PHP names to Novis ones, and there is none ([`programs/no-compatibility-promise`](programs.md#programs-no-compatibility-promise)).
- **A PHP name that resolves while the program runs, as an alias of a `Core` member.** It is a second
  name for one member ([`statements/nothing-gets-a-second-name`](statements.md#statements-nothing-gets-a-second-name)), and it keeps PHP names in
  committed source for good.
- **A `std::fs` listing in `completion.rs`.** It would bypass the test that keeps every completion
  source on a table the compiler builds, and could disagree with what resolution finds.
- **A completion file that overrides a method's return type.** The editor's types would then disagree
  with the compiler's, which is the second description of the program's shape this rule refuses.
- **Offering every workspace class for the string of `as class<T>`.** A class the program never loads
  is one the conversion throws for.
- **A bound in the class-name mark, so `assertThrows` would carry `Throwable` in the registry.** One
  member needs it, and a new mark field would be read by nothing but the editor.

<sub>See also [`ide/completion-files-offer-values-at-named-parameters`](ide.md#ide-completion-files-offer-values-at-named-parameters), [`routing/routes-are-compiled-not-registered`](routing.md#routing-routes-are-compiled-not-registered), [`routing/link-target-and-params-are-checked`](routing.md#routing-link-target-and-params-are-checked), [`config/a-duplicate-key-is-an-error-and-so-is-an-unknown-one`](config.md#config-a-duplicate-key-is-an-error-and-so-is-an-unknown-one), [`routing/api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table`](routing.md#routing-api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table), [`programs/no-first-party-framework`](programs.md#programs-no-first-party-framework).</sub>

<a id="ide-completion-files-offer-values-at-named-parameters"></a>

## A JSON file under a `.novis/completion` folder offers values at the string parameters it names, changes only the string the cursor is in, and is read and never run

`rule:ide/completion-files-offer-values-at-named-parameters`

A `.json` file under a folder named `.novis/completion/`, anywhere in the workspace and `vendor/`
included, is a completion file: data that names method parameters and the values the editor offers in a
string argument at them. Nothing in it is run, by the language server or by any later reader of
`.novis`, and the server makes no network request for it.

The values such a file lists are ones the program cannot see while it compiles: the modules a
deployment has, the names in an icon set, the keys of a dataset kept outside the repository. There is
no first description of them for the file to be a second, unchecked copy of, so
[`ide/completion-offers-only-what-the-compiler-derived`](ide.md#ide-completion-offers-only-what-the-compiler-derived) admits it as its one source of values the
compiler does not derive. Novis defines the file and nothing that writes it, so a Novis script, a
Python script, a CI job or a person can produce one, and nothing runs inside the editor. `.novis` is a
project's folder for data its tools read, found anywhere and as many times as a project needs, not an
editor's; each kind of data is a subfolder with its own format, so a later kind never shares a file
with this one, and any non-JSON file under `completion/` is ignored, so a README can sit beside the
data. It follows the dot-folder convention of `.vscode` and `.idea`, and is `novis` rather than `nvs`
because `.nvs` is the source file extension.

**What a file says.** The top-level fields are `$schema`, `sets` and `parameters`, and the field set is
closed at every level. A set is a name, shared across every completion file in the workspace, and a list
of values. A list is an array of values, or an object `{ "separator", "values" }` whose separator is
`.`, `/` or `:`. A value is a string, or an object whose one required field is `value`, the inserted
text, with the optional fields `label`, `labelDetail`, `labelDescription`, `kind`, `title`,
`documentation`, `deprecated`, `sortText`, `filterText` and `preselect`, each one field of an LSP
completion item, and two more: `location`, a `file` relative to the completion file's folder and a
1-based `line`, and `replacement`, the value that replaces a deprecated one. An attachment is a `method`
(`Class::method` with the class's whole name, a constructor as `Class::constructor`), a `parameter`
named without its `$`, a `set`, a list in `values` or both, and two optional fields: `when`, a
`parameter` of the same method and the string or strings its argument must `equals`, and `strict`.

Each optional field answers something a plain list cannot say. A translation key is defined in a file
of its own, and a developer reading it wants its text and the line that defines it: `location`. One
method's keys can depend on another argument, and a list merging every domain's keys offers mostly
wrong ones: `when`. Keys written as paths, with many entries under a few prefixes, are easier to choose
one segment at a time: a separator. A renamed value should say what replaced it: `replacement`.

**Where it reaches.** An attachment is keyed by the declaration the checker resolved the call to, so an
inherited method is reached through the class that declares it, and an override needs an attachment of
its own. An attachment with `when` applies at a call only when that call's argument for the named
parameter is a string literal equal to one of its strings, that argument found the way the completed
one is, so a named and a positional argument read alike; when that argument is not a literal or is
left out, only the attachments without `when` apply. Every applying attachment for one parameter
contributes, files in path order and entries in written order, and a repeated `value` keeps the first
one read. A set or a merge is never a conflict, so nothing about one is reported. Inside a string
argument at such a parameter, `'` and `"` open the list, as they do at a path or class-name parameter,
and a parameter a path or class-name mark already completes is offered both lists.

**What an item may do.** Its one edit replaces the text of the string literal with `value`, escaped for
the literal's quote style. In a list with a separator, completion offers the distinct segments that
follow the text already typed, and an item's edit replaces only the segment being typed. A segment
that ends a value carries that value's fields, and one that only leads to longer values carries its
text alone; the strict check and hover still compare whole values. The
separator, `.` included, opens the next segment's list inside such a string. No item carries a command,
which would let a cloned repository run an editor command when an item is accepted, an edit outside
