  simplicity priority does not pay for.
- **Opening a profile in speedscope.app.** It needs a browser and the network outside the editor, and
  the page cannot reach a file in a remote window.
- **A hand-rolled status-bar item for server health.** `LanguageStatusItem` is the API VS Code provides
  for exactly that.

<sub>See also [`ide/the-debug-adapter-does-not-wait-for-an-editor`](ide.md#ide-the-debug-adapter-does-not-wait-for-an-editor), [`testing/debug-probes`](testing.md#testing-debug-probes), [`testing/report-formats`](testing.md#testing-report-formats), [`ide/every-feature-is-staged-behind-its-dependency`](ide.md#ide-every-feature-is-staged-behind-its-dependency), [`observability/trace-events-carry-a-kind`](observability.md#observability-trace-events-carry-a-kind), [`ide/the-debugger-ui-is-as-deep-as-the-adapter`](ide.md#ide-the-debugger-ui-is-as-deep-as-the-adapter).</sub>

<a id="ide-a-file-shows-what-it-declares"></a>

## A file that declares one class, interface, enum or `type` alias and nothing else shows that kind beside its name as a letter, a file decoration with no colour that the server's `nvs/fileKinds` feeds

`rule:ide/a-file-shows-what-it-declares`

A file whose only declaration is one class, interface, enum or `type` alias, beside nothing but
`namespace` and `use`, shows that kind in the editor's file list as a letter beside its name: `C`, `I`,
`E` or `T`. That is the shape every autoloaded file
has ([`programs/one-declaration-per-autoloaded-file`](programs.md#programs-one-declaration-per-autoloaded-file)), and `nvs_hir::autoload::sole_declaration` is
the one scan both the shape check and this list read, so the shape the editor shows and the shape the
compiler accepts cannot disagree. A file reached by `require` with the same shape is listed as well: it
declares one thing just as plainly, and asking how a file was reached would need an edge the loaded
file does not keep.

The server answers `nvs/fileKinds` with every such file its index holds and the kind of each. The
request takes no parameters and answers `[{uri, kind}]`, `kind` being `class`, `interface`, `enum` or
`type`. The index records the kind as it reads the file, so an answer is one pass over its file map and
no analysis. The client never finds the kind itself by matching `class` or `enum` in the text, because
every judgement about the language stays in the server ([`ide/one-server-two-thin-clients`](ide.md#ide-one-server-two-thin-clients)). The
VS Code client draws the answer as a file decoration, the editor's own surface for a badge on a file
([`ide/the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has`](ide.md#ide-the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has)). The icon is unchanged: an editor picks
a file's icon from its name and language, never from its content. The decoration carries no colour,
because a decoration's colour is drawn on the file's name too, and a list of recoloured names is
harder to read than the names alone. With no colour the editor draws the letter in the name's own
colour, dimmed, the way a source-control letter looks on a file with no change colour. The letter and
the tooltip are the whole signal: a theme or a user cannot tell the kinds apart by colour. The stable
API takes a badge of one or two characters and draws no shape around it, and no API changes how the
Explorer shows a file's name.

The list is what the index holds. The client asks when a server starts answering, after
`nvs.checkWorkspace`, and when a Novis document is opened or saved, and several asks close together are
one, since the server does not watch `.nvs` files on disk. A file changed outside the editor shows its
old kind until one of those happens, the same staleness every reader of the index has. The badge shares
the decoration slot with source control, so a modified file may show the source-control badge in place
of its kind. No setting is added.

- **Memory:** one more field per indexed file in the server, for the life of the server process.
  Nothing at run time.

**Declined:**

- **The theme's symbol colour for each kind** (`symbolIcon.classForeground` and its siblings). The
  editor draws it on the name as well as the badge, so in a directory of autoloaded files nearly every
  name turned one of three colours, and the colours no longer marked anything out.
- **A circled or filled letter** (`Ⓒ`, `Ⓘ`, `Ⓔ`, `Ⓣ` and the negative circled letters). The circled
  ones looked worse than a plain letter, and the filled ones were too small to tell apart.
- **A badge drawn as an icon.** It is the proposed `codiconDecoration` API, which an extension published
  to the marketplace cannot use.
- **The kind in the file's name**, such as `Status.enum.nvs`. It would let an icon theme give each kind
  its own icon, but it changes how autoload finds a file, which every program's layout depends on, so it
  is a language decision and not an editor one.

<sub>See also [`programs/one-declaration-per-autoloaded-file`](programs.md#programs-one-declaration-per-autoloaded-file), [`ide/the-request-set-is-closed`](ide.md#ide-the-request-set-is-closed), [`ide/novis-ships-names-not-colours`](ide.md#ide-novis-ships-names-not-colours), [`ide/the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has`](ide.md#ide-the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has), [`ide/one-server-two-thin-clients`](ide.md#ide-one-server-two-thin-clients).</sub>

<a id="ide-the-test-tree-is-discovered-and-run-through-the-cli"></a>

## The Test Explorer is `nvs test --list` and `nvs test --format=json` projected: the client matches records to items and derives nothing

`rule:ide/the-test-tree-is-discovered-and-run-through-the-cli`

The Test Explorer is a projection of two documents the CLI writes: `nvs test --list --format=json`
fills the tree, and `nvs test --format=json --filter` runs a selection. A record is matched to a
`TestItem` by its `class` and `method`, and the file each item opens at is the `file`, `line` and
`column` the record carries — the client derives none of it.

Discovery must not run anything, which is why it is a flag on the runner rather than a run with every
test skipped: `--list` answers from the table the compile already built, so a workspace whose tests
fail, hang or `exit` populates a tree exactly as a passing one does. The `.nvst` corpus is the same
flag over each workspace folder: every `case` record is one leaf, and the client searches for no case
file itself. A workspace folder with programs and no case pays one compile of the folder as a
program for that listing, and the client reads none of its records.

Coverage is a third document from the same run. A run profile of kind `Coverage` beside the Run one
adds `--coverage-lcov` with a scratch file in the extension's storage directory and starts the run in
the program's workspace folder, which is what the tracefile's names are relative to
([`testing/coverage-report`](testing.md#testing-coverage-report)). Every `SF` record becomes one `FileCoverage` built from its `DA`
lines as statements, its `BRDA` sides as branches on the line they start on, and its `FN`/`FNDA` pairs
as declarations, so the totals VS Code shows are its own count of the runner's details. The extension
draws no gutter of its own ([`ide/the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has`](ide.md#ide-the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has)). The `.nvst`
corpus runs unchanged under that profile, because the CLI refuses a coverage flag over a case tree.

This is the shape [`ide/the-ast-panel-shells-out-to-the-cli`](ide.md#ide-the-ast-panel-shells-out-to-the-cli) already gives a view over compiler
tables: the binary answers, and the client renders. A client that scanned the workspace for test
classes itself would be a second implementation of the `#[Test]` table, free to disagree with the one
that runs.

**Declined:**
- **Asking the language server where a test is declared.** It is the client reconstructing what the
  CLI's document should carry, and a client feature whose CLI surface is missing is the CLI's to fix
  ([`ide/every-feature-is-staged-behind-its-dependency`](ide.md#ide-every-feature-is-staged-behind-its-dependency)).

<sub>See also [`testing/report-formats`](testing.md#testing-report-formats), [`ide/the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has`](ide.md#ide-the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has), [`ide/the-ast-panel-shells-out-to-the-cli`](ide.md#ide-the-ast-panel-shells-out-to-the-cli), [`ide/every-feature-is-staged-behind-its-dependency`](ide.md#ide-every-feature-is-staged-behind-its-dependency).</sub>

<a id="ide-the-ast-panel-shells-out-to-the-cli"></a>

## The AST panel renders `nvs ast --json` for the active file, on the resilient tree by default, and never runs `Core\Ast`

`rule:ide/the-ast-panel-shells-out-to-the-cli`

The AST explorer panel renders `nvs ast --json` for the active file as a tree view — the resilient tree
by default, so the panel works on a file that does not compile. `nvs ast` ships the `--json` flag with a
frozen schema for that purpose; the `{stmts:#?}` debug print has no stability contract and is not what
the panel reads.

The panel is off by default. The view and the command's palette entry are shown under `nvs.ast.enable`
(default `false`), because few users read a syntax tree and a view nobody opens should not take space
in every Explorer. The panel runs `nvs ast` only when **Novis: Show AST** is run, and again when the
file it shows is saved. Turning the setting off drops the tree it holds.

It does not use `Core\Ast` ([`core-classes/ast-is-inert`](core-classes.md#core-classes-ast-is-inert)). That is the language-level reflective
parse a running Novis program calls; the editor panel is simpler and shells out to the CLI, the same way
`nvs check` backs diagnostics. Both read the one tree there is ([`ide/one-grammar-one-tree`](ide.md#ide-one-grammar-one-tree)), so the
panel and the compiler cannot disagree about a file's shape.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/ast-is-inert`](core-classes.md#core-classes-ast-is-inert), [`ide/one-grammar-one-tree`](ide.md#ide-one-grammar-one-tree), [`ide/the-tree-survives-a-syntax-error`](ide.md#ide-the-tree-survives-a-syntax-error), [`ide/ast-json-schema-is-frozen`](ide.md#ide-ast-json-schema-is-frozen).</sub>

<a id="ide-the-lockfile-is-committed-and-build-output-is-not"></a>

## `package-lock.json` is committed; `node_modules/`, `out/`, `.vscode-test/` and `*.vsix` are ignored

`rule:ide/the-lockfile-is-committed-and-build-output-is-not`

`.gitignore` carries `node_modules/`, `out/`, `.vscode-test/` and `*.vsix`: a session that commits
`node_modules` is a session whose commit nobody can review. All four are anchored under `editors/` —
`/editors/*/out/` rather than `out/` — because the repository already has a documentation directory
named `out`, and an unanchored pattern silently stops tracking new files in it.

`package-lock.json` **is** committed, because `npm ci` is what the acceptance run uses and it requires one,
and because an unpinned dependency tree makes the grammar snapshots reproducible only by luck. CI carries
two jobs for the package beside the ones already there — `extension`, the headless suites on all three
platforms, and `extension-host` on Linux — and `ci.yml` is the count of those.

<sub>See also [`ide/headless-gates-the-loop-the-host-run-gates-the-milestone`](ide.md#ide-headless-gates-the-loop-the-host-run-gates-the-milestone), [`ide/the-extension-runs-where-the-binary-is`](ide.md#ide-the-extension-runs-where-the-binary-is).</sub>

<a id="ide-the-debug-adapter-does-not-wait-for-an-editor"></a>

## `nvs dap` launches `nvs run`, `nvs test` or a development `nvs serve` over stdio and never attaches; it is complete without any editor's debugger UI, and VS Code's wiring is a descriptor factory and a `launch.json` schema

`rule:ide/the-debug-adapter-does-not-wait-for-an-editor`

`nvs dap` — the debug adapter, stopping at the stop sites its debug compile switch puts at every
statement ([`testing/a-debugged-program-is-compiled-with-a-debug-switch`](testing.md#testing-a-debugged-program-is-compiled-with-a-debug-switch)) — is a complete, testable
deliverable on its own. A working adapter and a working debugger UI in a given editor
are two different integrations, the same way a language server and a syntax-highlighting extension are,
so a stalled or under-scoped editor integration cannot block the adapter from shipping and being useful
to a CLI-driven client or a third editor.

**It launches, and never attaches.** `nvs dap` speaks DAP over its own stdin and stdout and answers
`launch` alone: it compiles the program with the switch and runs it in its own process, as `nvs run`,
`nvs test` or `nvs serve` would. A launched `nvs serve` starts in `development` whatever `[mode] default`
says, and a breakpoint stops whichever request reaches it while every other request is served
([`testing/a-stop-pauses-the-whole-task-tree`](testing.md#testing-a-stop-pauses-the-whole-task-tree)). There is no `attach` request, so no running process
ever listens for a debugger and there is no debug socket to bind, guard or forget open. A production
server cannot be debugged, which is the point: the switch slows every statement and a stop holds a
request.

stdout carries DAP frames and nothing else, on the terms
[`ide/stdout-belongs-to-the-protocol`](ide.md#ide-stdout-belongs-to-the-protocol) sets for the language server. What the launched program
writes to its stdout and stderr reaches the client as `output` events, so a program that prints a
frame-shaped line shows text and cannot speak the protocol.

The `launch` arguments are the whole interface: `mode` (`run`, `test` or `serve`), `program`, `args`,
`cwd`, `env`, `stopOnEntry`, the test `filter` under `test`, `skipFiles` and `pathMappings`
([`ide/the-debugger-ui-is-as-deep-as-the-adapter`](ide.md#ide-the-debugger-ui-is-as-deep-as-the-adapter)). `nvsCommand`, read by the editor and never by
the adapter, names the command that starts `nvs dap`, so the adapter can run inside a container through
`docker exec -i` and still be reached over stdio.

For VS Code the editor-side wiring is small and lands with the adapter: a `DebugAdapterDescriptorFactory`
and a `launch.json` configuration schema targeting `nvs dap`. DAP is a wire protocol, and VS Code
already renders breakpoints, call stack, variables and watches for any adapter that speaks it, so the
extension authors no debugger UI — the acceptance is a breakpoint set in VS Code's UI hitting in
JIT-compiled code with correct variable values, through the descriptor factory and schema alone
([`ide/the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has`](ide.md#ide-the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has)). How deep that UI goes is the adapter's
capability set, not the extension's.


- **Memory:** the adapter's own state is one entry per breakpoint and one per stopped thread's
  variable references, freed on each resume. What the debugged program holds is the switch's
  ([`testing/a-debugged-program-is-compiled-with-a-debug-switch`](testing.md#testing-a-debugged-program-is-compiled-with-a-debug-switch)).

**`nvsCommand` is a binary or a command line.** A string names an `nvs` binary, which the extension
runs a copy of like every other spawn ([`ide/the-extension-runs-a-copy-of-the-binary`](ide.md#ide-the-extension-runs-a-copy-of-the-binary)). An
array is a whole command line, such as `["docker", "exec", "-i", "app", "nvs"]`, and runs as written
with `dap` appended: its first word is a wrapper, not an `nvs` build, so there is nothing to copy.

**Built:** `nvs dap` (`crates/nvs-cli/src/dap/`), which drives `nvs_host::debug`'s controller, and
the VS Code wiring: the `debuggers` contribution in `editors/vscode/package.json` and the factory in
`editors/vscode/src/debug.ts`. `crates/nvs-cli/tests/dap.rs` drives the adapter as a client does,
and `editors/vscode/test/host/surfaces.test.ts` stops at a breakpoint set through VS Code's API.

**Declined:**
- **The adapter ships together with an editor's debugger UI.** A stalled editor integration would hold
  back an adapter that a CLI-driven client can already use.
- **`attach` to a running server.** It needs a listener in every process that might be debugged, with
  its own authentication, and a production process with that listener is one misconfiguration from
  handing out its memory. Launching gives the same view of a development server with no listener.
- **Running the program as a child process of the adapter.** The adapter would need a second protocol
  to the child to reach its stops, and in one process the controller is a Rust call.

<sub>See also [`ide/the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has`](ide.md#ide-the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has), [`testing/debug-probes`](testing.md#testing-debug-probes), [`ide/the-debugger-ui-is-as-deep-as-the-adapter`](ide.md#ide-the-debugger-ui-is-as-deep-as-the-adapter), [`testing/a-debugged-program-is-compiled-with-a-debug-switch`](testing.md#testing-a-debugged-program-is-compiled-with-a-debug-switch), [`testing/a-stop-pauses-the-whole-task-tree`](testing.md#testing-a-stop-pauses-the-whole-task-tree), [`ide/stdout-belongs-to-the-protocol`](ide.md#ide-stdout-belongs-to-the-protocol).</sub>

<a id="ide-the-debugger-ui-is-as-deep-as-the-adapter"></a>

## The debugger UI is only as deep as the capabilities `nvs dap` reports, so the adapter's capability list is the debugger's scope

`rule:ide/the-debugger-ui-is-as-deep-as-the-adapter`

`nvs dap` is wired into VS Code's existing debugger UI, and every feature below renders in a UI that
already exists — it appears only if the adapter reports the corresponding capability at `initialize`. The
adapter's capability list is therefore the debugger's scope, and it is this:

- **Stepping over, into and out, one statement at a time** — `next`, `stepIn` and `stepOut` move a
  thread to its next stop site in the same frame, in any deeper frame, or in its caller. A step over an
  `await` stops at the next statement of the same frame once that task resumes, and the other tasks run
  while it waits. A step into a call through a `callable` lands in the function or closure it names. A
  step into a `Core` method steps over it, because it has no stop sites.
- **Conditional breakpoints, hit counts and logpoints** — `supportsConditionalBreakpoints`,
  `supportsHitConditionalBreakpoints`, `supportsLogPoints`. A logpoint that does not stop the program is
  the debugging most users actually do.
- **Exception filters** — `exceptionBreakpointFilters`, so "break on uncaught" and "break on thrown" are
  separate switches. [`errors/escalation-ladder`](errors.md#errors-escalation-ladder)'s single `Throwable` channel is what makes this two
  filters and no more.
- **Stepping exclusions** — `skipFiles`, a `launch.json` glob list, so stepping does not descend into
  package code and a handled throw inside it does not stop the session.
- **Path mappings**, because the container case is the normal case: the file the adapter reports and the
  file in the editor differ whenever the program runs anywhere but the workspace root. `pathMappings`
  pairs an editor folder with the adapter's, as `{ "localRoot", "remoteRoot" }`, and every path in and
  out of the adapter is mapped: `program`, `cwd` and each breakpoint's file in, each frame's file out.
  The longest root that matches whole parts of a path wins, and a `skipFiles` glob is matched against
  the editor's path, since it is written in `launch.json` beside the rest.
- **The value a function just returned**, in the variables pane after stepping out. It is one frame's
  worth of state the adapter already has, and the UI renders it with no work of its own.
- **Every task of the debugged request is a DAP thread**, a `spawn`ed isolate's included, and a stop
  pauses all of them ([`testing/a-stop-pauses-the-whole-task-tree`](testing.md#testing-a-stop-pauses-the-whole-task-tree)). That is the standard
  presentation, needing no protocol extension. The *tree* of tasks would need one and is not built.

**A condition and a logpoint's `{…}` hole are expressions over the stopped frame's variables.** They
are type-checked against the frame's slot table
([`testing/a-debugged-program-is-compiled-with-a-debug-switch`](testing.md#testing-a-debugged-program-is-compiled-with-a-debug-switch)) when the breakpoint is set, and a
condition must be a `bool`. They may read variables, properties and array elements, and use literals,
operators and comparisons. They may not call a function or a method, assign, or `await`, so a
breakpoint never changes what the program does. A call is an error the editor shows: a condition or
hole that does not compile leaves its breakpoint unverified, with the compiler's message. A hit
condition is `N`, `>N`, `>=N`, `==N` or `%N`, counted per breakpoint.

**"Uncaught" is decided where the exception is thrown,** while every frame is still there to show. Under
the switch the compiler records which classes the `try` blocks around each statement catch, and each
frame record names the statement it is at, so the adapter knows at the throw whether any frame of that
task will catch it. A frame in a `skipFiles` file that catches it means the throw does not stop.

A fixture session exercises each of these, and `nvs dap` reports each capability at `initialize`.

- **Memory:** per stopped thread, one variable reference per expanded value, freed on resume; per
  breakpoint, its compiled condition and its hit count.

**Built:** every capability above, in `crates/nvs-cli/src/dap/`: steps through `nvs_host::debug`'s
`Debugger::step`, conditions and logpoints in `condition.rs` over `nvs_types::condition`'s checker,
the exception filters through `nvs_debug_throw`, the returned value in `stopped.rs`, and the path
mappings in `paths.rs`. `crates/nvs-cli/tests/dap.rs` is the fixture session.

**Declined:**
- **A condition that calls a function.** The call could write, throw or `await` at a breakpoint, and the
  program would then behave differently under the debugger than without it.
- **Deciding "uncaught" when the exception leaves the last frame.** The frames are gone by then, and the
  stop would show where the task ended instead of where it threw.

<sub>See also [`errors/escalation-ladder`](errors.md#errors-escalation-ladder), [`security/isolate-shares-nothing`](security.md#security-isolate-shares-nothing), [`ide/every-feature-is-staged-behind-its-dependency`](ide.md#ide-every-feature-is-staged-behind-its-dependency), [`testing/a-debugged-program-is-compiled-with-a-debug-switch`](testing.md#testing-a-debugged-program-is-compiled-with-a-debug-switch), [`testing/a-stop-pauses-the-whole-task-tree`](testing.md#testing-a-stop-pauses-the-whole-task-tree).</sub>

<a id="ide-stdout-belongs-to-the-protocol"></a>

## Nothing but the protocol writes to the server's stdout; logging goes to stderr and `window/logMessage`

`rule:ide/stdout-belongs-to-the-protocol`

stdio *is* the wire. One stray `println!` anywhere under the analysis corrupts the framing, which presents
as the server dying for no reason. So nothing but the protocol may write to stdout: the server logs to
stderr and, for anything a user should see, `window/logMessage`, and `nvs-lsp` does not carry `nvs-cli`'s
`clippy::print_stdout` allowance.

`println!`/`print!` appears nowhere in `crates/` outside `nvs-cli`, whose whole job is terminal
output, so this is an invariant to keep rather than one to establish, and it is kept by a test over
every crate the server links rather than by care. The server links the type checker, so `nvs-stdlib`
and `nvs-runtime` beneath it are in that dependency set, and the runtime does write to stdout: it is where a
program's `echo` goes under `nvs run`. That is not an exception, because it is a sink a caller wires
into a `Ctx` and the server builds no `Ctx` at all — so the test exempts the sink's own
implementation and separately checks that nothing under the server wires one.

<sub>See also [`ide/the-server-is-synchronous`](ide.md#ide-the-server-is-synchronous).</sub>

<a id="ide-the-extension-refuses-a-binary-it-does-not-understand"></a>

## On a version mismatch at `initialize` the client says so in the status item and does not start

`rule:ide/the-extension-refuses-a-binary-it-does-not-understand`

`nvs lsp` reports its version at `initialize`. On a mismatch with the extension's own, the
`LanguageStatusItem` says so and the client does not start, rather than running and producing confusing
answers.

An old `nvs` earlier on `PATH` than the intended one is the single most likely support question this
extension will ever get, and it costs one comparison to answer it out loud. A client reporting a mismatched
version gets a refusal and a status item, not a session.

<sub>See also [`ide/the-extension-runs-where-the-binary-is`](ide.md#ide-the-extension-runs-where-the-binary-is), [`ide/the-server-is-synchronous`](ide.md#ide-the-server-is-synchronous).</sub>

<a id="ide-the-extension-runs-a-copy-of-the-binary"></a>

## Every process the extension starts runs from a verified copy of the binary that is never older than the build on disk, so the file the user named is never held

`rule:ide/the-extension-runs-a-copy-of-the-binary`

The VS Code extension never runs the binary `nvs.path` or `PATH` names: every process it starts — the
server, the Tasks, the formatter, the AST panel and the test controller — runs from a verified copy of
that binary in the extension's own storage, and the copy is never an older build than the one on disk.
The server lives as long as the window and a program in a Task's terminal as long as the user leaves it,
and every platform guards the file of a running program — Windows refuses to overwrite or delete it,
Linux fails a write into it with *Text file busy*, macOS may kill a signed process whose file is
rewritten — so an editor that ran the named file would turn being open into a build or an upgrade that
cannot write its output.

**The copy and the binary are the same program, or the copy is not used.** A copy is handed out only
after both files have been hashed and found equal and the binary's size and modification time have been
read again and found unchanged, whether the copy was just made or was already there. A copy taken while
a linker is still writing is discarded and made again. The copy is named for the binary's path, size and
modification time, so every window on one build shares one file and no window replaces a file another is
running.

**Every spawn asks which file to run at the moment it spawns**, in one place, `src/binary.ts`. The answer
is the remembered copy only while the binary and the copy both still read the size and modification time
they had when they were hashed — two `stat`s — and anything else is a new verified copy before the
process starts. A Task is the one thing that carries a path for longer than a spawn, because the editor
keeps Task objects of its own; one started over the copy of an earlier build is stopped and run again
over the current one.

**A changed binary takes over the server within seconds, and the user sees nothing.** The extension reads
the binary's size and modification time once a second, and acts when a reading differs from the running
build and equals the reading before it; the second equal reading keeps it off a half-written file. It
polls rather than subscribing because the file is replaced, not edited, and one `stat` a second behaves
the same on every platform, network mount and WSL path. The new copy is made and verified and the new
server started and its version compared ([`ide/the-extension-refuses-a-binary-it-does-not-understand`](ide.md#ide-the-extension-refuses-a-binary-it-does-not-understand))
while the old server is still answering, and only then is the old one stopped, so there is no gap in
diagnostics or completion and the status item never leaves its resting state. **A server that is
answering is the build on disk, or there is no server**: when the new build will not start or is refused,
the old one is stopped all the same and the status item says why. The watch is set whatever the start
came to, so the rebuild of a binary that would not start is picked up without being asked for.

Where no copy can be made, or the copy will not start — storage mounted `noexec` — the named binary is
run and the status item says that file is being held, and why. There is no setting for any of this.
Copies live under `server/` in the extension's global storage, which is on the machine the code is on
([`ide/the-extension-is-a-workspace-extension`](ide.md#ide-the-extension-is-a-workspace-extension)); a copy of an earlier build of the same binary is
deleted when a new one is made, a copy of some other binary once it is a week old, and a file another
window is running is left for the next sweep, and so is any file this module did not write.

A copy is the same program in the two places `nvs` reads its own file. A bundle's payload is read from
the end of the running executable, which a byte copy keeps. The compile cache's build stamp hashes the
executable's path, length and modification time, so a copy keys apart from its binary: one cold compile
for each new build, and the same key on every later run of that copy. A new build costs one copy and two
hashes of `nvs`, once per window; every other spawn costs two `stat`s, and nothing is on a request path.
For the moment two servers answer, a request may be answered by both.

**Memory:** nothing beyond a second server process for the moment of a switch. It spends disk instead:
one file the size of `nvs` for each binary in use, under the extension's storage.

**Declined:**
- **Copying on Windows only.** The lock is not only Windows', the stale server is every platform's, and
  a branch taken on one platform is one the other platforms' test runs never execute.
- **Copying only for the server.** A program in an `nvs run` Task runs as long as the server does, and
  "the editor never holds the binary" is a rule a user can rely on where "only sometimes" is not.
- **Renaming the old binary aside when updating.** Windows allows renaming a running executable, but it
  does nothing for a `nvs.path` pointed into `target/`, where the linker writes the file.
- **`nvs lsp` copying and re-executing itself.** The editor tracks the process it spawned, so the parent
  stays alive, and the parent is the file that is held.
- **A command that stops the server.** It needs the user to remember the cause, which is what keeps not
  happening.
- **Stopping the old server before starting the new one.** It costs a gap in diagnostics and completion
  on every rebuild.
- **Keeping the old server when the new build fails.** Its answers would come from a program that is no
  longer on disk.
- **Naming the copy for a hash of its content.** That needs the binary hashed before there is a name to
  look for; the stamp gives the name for one `stat`, and the hash still decides whether the file is used.
- **A setting to turn it off.** The fallback is automatic, and a setting is kept forever.

<sub>See also [`ide/the-extension-refuses-a-binary-it-does-not-understand`](ide.md#ide-the-extension-refuses-a-binary-it-does-not-understand), [`ide/the-extension-guides-an-install-and-never-bundles-one`](ide.md#ide-the-extension-guides-an-install-and-never-bundles-one), [`ide/the-extension-is-a-workspace-extension`](ide.md#ide-the-extension-is-a-workspace-extension).</sub>

<a id="ide-dependencies-are-allowlisted"></a>

## The extension holds no language logic, and its `package.json` dependencies are checked against an allowlist by its own tests

`rule:ide/dependencies-are-allowlisted`

The extension may hold no language logic — no parser, no formatter, no type table — and this is enforced
rather than intended: its `package.json` `dependencies` are checked against an allowlist by its own test
suite, so a second implementation cannot arrive as a dependency, and the reviewer is not the only thing
standing between the repository and one.

The same allowlist is what keeps the client free of language logic when a feature is added. The redaction
of [`ide/redaction-ranges-come-from-the-server`](ide.md#ide-redaction-ranges-come-from-the-server) is a range list from the server and a decoration;
there is nothing in it a parser would help with, and the test is unchanged by it.

<sub>See also [`ide/contributions-are-frozen-and-only-ever-added`](ide.md#ide-contributions-are-frozen-and-only-ever-added), [`ide/headless-gates-the-loop-the-host-run-gates-the-milestone`](ide.md#ide-headless-gates-the-loop-the-host-run-gates-the-milestone), [`ide/redaction-ranges-come-from-the-server`](ide.md#ide-redaction-ranges-come-from-the-server), [`ide/one-server-two-thin-clients`](ide.md#ide-one-server-two-thin-clients).</sub>

<a id="ide-redaction-ranges-come-from-the-server"></a>

## The editor conceals a `secret` value by default, and the ranges come from the language server rather than a client guess

`rule:ide/redaction-ranges-come-from-the-server`

A `secret` value is concealed in the editor by default. The language server answers a list of ranges
and their kinds; the client draws them and knows nothing about what a secret is, because the
alternative is the client guessing.

**The server can be exact where a client cannot.** A tool that hides secrets in an editor otherwise
guesses, by filename, by pattern or by entropy. `secret` is a type-checker fact, and it propagates
through concatenation and interpolation ([`security/secret-propagation`](security.md#security-secret-propagation)), so a value derived from a
credential is concealed for the same reason the credential is, with no heuristic involved. A guess would
miss every value that became `secret` by propagation, which is most of them.

The threat this closes is an **incidental viewer**: a stream, a screen share, a screenshot, somebody
looking over a shoulder. It is not a defence against the machine's own user and it is not secret
management.

**This is a rendering, and it is not what makes a `secret` safe.** The language's guarantee is that
every sink refuses one ([`security/secret-sinks-refuse`](security.md#security-secret-sinks-refuse)), checked by the compiler, with no editor
involved and nothing an editor could weaken. Concealment covers the one exposure a compiler cannot
reach — a value legible on a screen somebody else is looking at — and it covers nothing else. An
editor drawing no decoration at all is not running a less safe language; it is only less discreet,
which is why every rule in this section is the editor's and none of them is the language's.

The test that puts a rule here rather than under `security/` is whether it still holds with no editor
running. Every sink refusing a `secret` does, and so do the AST dump's placeholder
([`security/redaction-reaches-the-tools-own-renderings`](security.md#security-redaction-reaches-the-tools-own-renderings)) and the test runner's redacted diff
([`security/secret-in-a-test-report`](security.md#security-secret-in-a-test-report)). A blur over a string literal does not. The security chapter
is read as what the language will not let a program get wrong, and a rendering filed there would invite
a reader to count it as part of that guarantee.

It does **not** ride the semantic-token channel, even though the qualifier already travels there. That
channel's contract is *names a theme styles*, and its correct degradation is to fall back to the
underlying token type — which a security default whose failure mode is *the value becomes visible*
cannot inherit. Two mechanisms, two contracts, and neither can silently disable the other.

The fail direction is named, because mid-edit is exactly when the type is unknown. A range whose
expression cannot be typed, but whose **binding's declared type carries `secret`**, is redacted
anyway; the client **holds its last answer** and never clears decorations on an error, a cancellation
or a restart. An empty answer means nothing to redact; a *missing* answer means nothing at all.

Redacting on the declared type when the expression's own type is unknown is an over-approximation, and
it is kept because the other failure, the value flashing visible on every keystroke inside a string being
typed, is the one that loses the credential. Where the server cannot attribute a range at all, it answers
nothing for it and the value is visible. That gap is the honest one: over-redacting a document that does
not parse would conceal arbitrary spans of a file somebody is trying to fix.

The cost is a second decoration mechanism beside the semantic-token one, with two contracts to keep
apart and two ways for one token to be described.

- **Memory:** none on the request path. The server answers a range list per open document, and the
  client keeps the last answer for each.

**Declined:**

- **Detecting the range in the client** with a pattern or a filename rule. It puts language logic in a
  client ([`ide/one-server-two-thin-clients`](ide.md#ide-one-server-two-thin-clients)), and it misses every value that is `secret` by
  propagation.
- **A third semantic-token modifier.** That channel degrades to the underlying token type when a theme
  has no opinion, and a security default may not have un-redacting as its degradation.
- **Serving a redacted document** through a content provider or a custom editor. The file stops being an
  editable text document, with no language-server edits, no diff, no version-control integration and no
  format-on-save, which is a far larger loss than the exposure it closes; and it substitutes the buffer,
  which [`ide/redaction-covers-bytes-only`](ide.md#ide-redaction-covers-bytes-only) rules out.
- **A chapter of its own for security in the editor.** It splits the editor across two homes, and every
  rule in each would need a pointer to the other. The editor's chapter is the one home for the editor,
  and its security rules sit together at its end.

<sub>See also [`ide/redaction-covers-bytes-only`](ide.md#ide-redaction-covers-bytes-only), [`ide/reveal-is-explicit-and-window-local`](ide.md#ide-reveal-is-explicit-and-window-local), [`ide/redaction-does-not-reach`](ide.md#ide-redaction-does-not-reach).</sub>

<a id="ide-redaction-covers-bytes-only"></a>

## Only the bytes are concealed — a literal token or an interpolation slot, never an identifier or an annotation

`rule:ide/redaction-covers-bytes-only`

A range is answered when it is a string, heredoc or `bytes` literal token whose static type carries
`secret`, or an interpolation slot inside one whose interpolated expression does. Nothing else.

**Never an identifier** — a variable or property name is a name, not a secret, and concealing it hides
no bytes while making the file unreadable for the developer whose editor it is. **Never a type
annotation** — `secret string` is the declaration doing its job, and it is how a reader knows the
concealment below it is deliberate rather than a rendering fault. **Never a whole line, statement or
block**, which line-granular folding structurally cannot express anyway.

The concealment is a decoration over the range with the character cells kept, so the cursor, the
selection and every edit still address the real text. It is a rendering, not an edit: the buffer is
the file on disk, byte for byte.

The range is this narrow because the qualifiers propagate: in a request handler nearly every string
expression carries one, so concealing or marking every qualified expression would bury the file and be
turned off, taking the redaction with it.

**Declined:**

- **Folding the value away.** Folding is line-granular, so it cannot express a literal inside a one-line
  declaration such as `secret string $k = "…";`, which is the shape this exists for; and it would hide
  the declaration itself, which stays legible.
- **Removing the span from layout** (`display: none`) instead of blurring it. Removing the box breaks
  cursor and selection arithmetic across the range, and the editor has to keep behaving like a text
  editor.

<sub>See also [`ide/redaction-ranges-come-from-the-server`](ide.md#ide-redaction-ranges-come-from-the-server), [`security/secret-qualifier`](security.md#security-secret-qualifier).</sub>

<a id="ide-reveal-is-explicit-and-window-local"></a>

## A reveal is per range, window-local, and does not survive the editor closing

`rule:ide/reveal-is-explicit-and-window-local`

A reveal is per range, window-local, and dropped when the editor for that document closes. It is not
written to workspace state and does not survive a reload.

The threat model is an unattended screen, so a reveal that outlives the moment it was needed is the
same as no redaction at all — and a user who revealed one credential to read it has not consented to
reveal every credential in the workspace for the rest of the week.

There are three ways to ask, and they divide on what they leave behind rather than on how they are
spelled. The hover's command link and the `nvs.revealSecret` command are **held**: the range stays
uncovered until the editor closes or `nvs.hideSecrets` runs, so each one is a decision the user made
about one range and can be pointed at afterwards. **A cursor inside a range uncovers it and holds
nothing** — the range is covered again the instant the cursor leaves, and nothing anywhere records
that it was ever uncovered.

The cursor is admitted because it cannot leave a screen uncovered behind the user. A held reveal
can: it survives every scroll, edit and tab switch until the window is told otherwise, which is
exactly the exposure the paragraph above is about. A reveal that is a function of where the caret is
right now expires on the next arrow key, so the worst it can do is show the value the user is
already looking at. That is a smaller surface than the two held reveals it sits beside, not a larger
one — the reason to write it down is that it *reads* like the opposite.

There is still **no automatic reveal and no automatic re-conceal on a signal**, because there is no
signal: nothing reports that a window is being shared, recorded or projected. Anything that looked like
one would be a guess with a security failure attached, so redaction is unconditional by default and the
user is the only thing that turns it off, with `nvs.secrets.redact` (default `true`).

**Declined:**

- **Redacting only while the screen is shared.** No editor API reports it, so this would be a guess
  whose failure is a leaked credential.
- **A reveal that persists** in workspace state or across a reload. It outlives the moment it was
  needed, which is the exposure this rule exists to close.

<sub>See also [`ide/redaction-ranges-come-from-the-server`](ide.md#ide-redaction-ranges-come-from-the-server), [`ide/redaction-does-not-reach`](ide.md#ide-redaction-does-not-reach).</sub>

<a id="ide-redaction-does-not-reach"></a>

## What the editor's concealment cannot cover is written down, because a redaction trusted past its reach is worse than none

`rule:ide/redaction-does-not-reach`

The concealment is cosmetic, and what it cannot cover is written down and shipped in the tool's own
documentation, because a redaction trusted past its reach is worse than none.

Workspace search results and quick-open previews render matching lines outside any editor, so no
decoration applies. Diff and version-control views can be decorated, but there is no type information
for the "before" side, so the old value of an edited secret is visible in the review of that edit. The
minimap renders from the buffer. Any other extension's hover, lens or webview reads the document text
directly. A copy of a concealed range copies the plaintext, and nothing may intercept the clipboard.
And the file itself is on disk, in the working tree, and in the history the moment it is committed —
concealing a hardcoded credential does not make it less hardcoded.

This list is part of the decision, not commentary on it, and it is the real cost of the feature: a user
who believes the editor protects them everywhere is worse off than one who knows it does not.

**Declined:**

- **Intercepting copy** by rebinding the editor's copy action. It overrides a global keybinding for the
  whole editor to protect a value that is on disk anyway, and a redaction that fights the user's own
  clipboard is past the threat of an incidental viewer.
- **Refusing or warning on a `secret`-typed source literal in `nvs check`**, the cause the concealment
  only treats. Does not exist: the checker holds both facts it would need, but a test fixture, an example
  and a conformance case all legitimately write one.
- **Redacting the "before" side of a diff.** Does not exist: it needs a type answer for a revision of the
  document the server never analysed.

**Built:** the concealment itself ([`ide/redaction-ranges-come-from-the-server`](ide.md#ide-redaction-ranges-come-from-the-server)), and this list in
`editors/vscode/README.md` § *Where hidden secrets are still visible*, the page the Marketplace shows.

<sub>See also [`ide/redaction-ranges-come-from-the-server`](ide.md#ide-redaction-ranges-come-from-the-server), [`ide/reveal-is-explicit-and-window-local`](ide.md#ide-reveal-is-explicit-and-window-local).</sub>

<a id="ide-tainted-has-no-default-decoration"></a>

## `tainted` ships no default editor decoration, and the marker is opt-in

`rule:ide/tainted-has-no-default-decoration`

`tainted` gets a semantic-token modifier and **no default decoration**. A marker glyph is added
content rather than a colour, and shipping one on by default writes into someone else's editor exactly
what the token-modifier rule refuses. The marker is `nvs.taint.mark`, and `off` is the default:

| Value | What is marked |
|---|---|
| `off` | nothing; the token modifier alone, styled by the theme |
| `declaration` | a glyph after each declaration whose type carries `tainted` |
| `sink` | `declaration`, plus each argument position where a `tainted` value reaches a sink under [`security/sink-predicate`](security.md#security-sink-predicate) |

Only a declaration is marked, never a use: a `tainted` value is tainted at every use, so a glyph per
use would mark most of a request handler and teach nothing. Where the marker is on, the glyph is one
plain text character in the editor's own font rather than an emoji, which renders at the mercy of the
installed fonts and can show as a replacement box; its colour is a theme reference rather than a
literal. It is not an icon image, because an inline image takes no theme colour and would ship a colour
of Novis's own ([`ide/novis-ships-names-not-colours`](ide.md#ide-novis-ships-names-not-colours)). Until the sink classification exists on the
`Core` member rows, `sink` marks what `declaration` does.

The cost is a setting that ships inert by default, and that still costs documentation and a test.

**The asymmetry with `secret` is the whole content of this rule.** A credential on a shared screen is
a security incident, which is what buys `secret` its default
([`ide/redaction-ranges-come-from-the-server`](ide.md#ide-redaction-ranges-come-from-the-server)). A tainted value on a screen is not an event
at all: `tainted` is a compile-time guarantee already enforced by refusing the sink
([`security/sink-predicate`](security.md#security-sink-predicate)), so marking it is teaching, and teaching does not get to override the
user's theme.

**Declined:**

- **The marker on by default.** It overrides the user's theme for something that is not a security
  event, and since every `Core\Request` accessor returns `tainted`, most string expressions in a request
  handler would carry it. The default would bury the file, and the setting that turns it off would take
  the `secret` redaction with it in the user's mind.

<sub>See also [`ide/redaction-ranges-come-from-the-server`](ide.md#ide-redaction-ranges-come-from-the-server), [`security/sink-predicate`](security.md#security-sink-predicate), [`security/tainted-qualifier`](security.md#security-tainted-qualifier).</sub>

<a id="ide-a-hover-shows-where-a-tainted-or-secret-value-came-from"></a>

## Hovering a `tainted` or `secret` value shows its path inside the method, from where the qualifier entered to the cursor with the launderer marked, and only the language server has the checker record it

`rule:ide/a-hover-shows-where-a-tainted-or-secret-value-came-from`

Hovering a value whose type carries `tainted` or `secret`, or an argument where such a value reaches a
sink, shows the path the qualifier took inside the method: where it entered, each step that carried
it, and the call that laundered it, each with its line. The checker records that path only under a
switch that `nvs-lsp` alone sets, so a compile for running, `nvs check` and `nvs build` record nothing.

A path starts where the qualifier entered the method: a source ([`security/tainted-sources`](security.md#security-tainted-sources)), a
conversion out of `mixed` ([`security/taint-propagation`](security.md#security-taint-propagation)), or a parameter, property or return type
declared with the qualifier. Each assignment, concatenation and interpolation that carried it is a
step. A launderer ([`security/launderers-are-sink-named`](security.md#security-launderers-are-sink-named)) is the step where the qualifier ended,
and the hover marks it.

The path stops at the method's boundary. A qualifier crosses a boundary only through a declared type,
so a parameter declared `tainted` is where the value entered this method, and the hover names that
declaration. That declaration is everything the method knows about its caller.

- **Memory:** under the switch, one list of steps per qualified value, bounded by the statements of its
  method and freed with the analysis in the editor process. Without the switch, one predicted branch per
  recording site at compile time, and nothing at run time.

**Declined:**
- **Recording the path on every compile.** Nothing but the editor reads it.
- **A path across methods.** It would be a whole-program flow analysis, and the declared qualifier on
  a parameter already states what crosses.
- **A panel or a request of its own for the path.** A hover is a surface every editor has
  ([`ide/the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has`](ide.md#ide-the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has)).

<sub>See also [`security/tainted-sources`](security.md#security-tainted-sources), [`security/launderers-are-sink-named`](security.md#security-launderers-are-sink-named), [`security/taint-propagation`](security.md#security-taint-propagation), [`ide/tainted-has-no-default-decoration`](ide.md#ide-tainted-has-no-default-decoration), [`ide/the-request-set-is-closed`](ide.md#ide-the-request-set-is-closed).</sub>
